t: What a Shadow AI Audit Would Catch in Your Company
q: The model didn't stay in the sandbox. It found a flaw, broke out, used stolen login credentials, and hacked its way into Hugging Face (one of the largest platforms in the AI world, where companies host their models and data).

Here's the part worth sitting with. The model completed its task. It did what it was asked. It just did it the way a criminal would, through theft and a break-in, because no one had set clear parameters telling it what was off-limits. A person who pulled that off would be in handcuffs. The AI logged it as a job well done.

What that story actually shows is simpler and closer to home: a capable tool with no clear parameters will reach the goal in ways you never authorized. That's true for a billion-dollar lab, and it's just as true for a five-person nonprofit using a free chatbot.

Here's the analogy I use with leaders. Bringing AI into your organization with no parameters is like handing a brilliant new hire the keys to the building, the logins to every system, and a goal, all on their first day, with no rules of engagement and no background check.

Where a tool is allowed to reach, what data is off-limits, which accounts are acceptable: none of that gets settled in the server room. Those are leadership calls, and they have to be made before the tool shows up, not after.

In IBM's Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025, organizations with high levels of shadow AI paid an average of $4.74 million per breach, compared with $4.07 million for those with little or none, a $670,000 penalty for not knowing what your people were running.

t: What Career Emergence Actually Feels Like
q: The career version is the idea that instead of trying to design your career toward a clear long-term plan, you can clarify your principles, focus on the right next step, and trust that something you could never have planned might emerge.
At some point, I started using the word "Joy" as my compass: the work I would want to do even if no one was noticing. That sounds slightly woo-woo, but it became incredibly practical.

The hardest part was that I had no external evidence that I was going in the right direction. There was no promotion or title or salary increase telling me, "Good job, keep going." I had to trust my own compass—which sounds lovely when I write it now and felt fucking terrible at the time.

It is so important to be wary of decisions that are a "one-way door" (hard to take back) in the wandering phase. Anything reversible is your friend; anything permanent might just be a temporary fix for your anxiety, not a long-term happy place.

That conversation eventually led to TED offering me the opportunity to take over as host of WorkLife, the podcast they'd built with Adam Grant over the previous seven years. WorkLife was not unlikely to be in my five-year plan. It was impossible to be in my five-year plan.

All I could do was pay attention to what gave me energy, say no when something felt wrong even when I couldn't fully explain why, and keep choosing the next step that felt right. And then, eventually, the pattern emerged.

t: Visualizing the AI Education Debate
q: On Substack and other social platforms, the discourse is dominated by one-point solutions. "Cultivate AI literacy." "Redesign instruction." "Track metacognition." "Grade process." "Detect student use of AI." "Return to the analog classroom." Every few months, the cycle repeats.

As attractive as the framework is, though, I worry about the way it may inadvertently keep us locked inside the rhetoric of thesis and antithesis. If we are truly grappling with wicked problems, why strive toward common solutions at all?

A ban limits sanctioned use in school while students continue to use AI elsewhere, which can eventually create pressure to reopen access. Open access without instructional redesign increases concerns about student offloading and produces pressure to restrict.

The problem repeatedly migrates upward in scale. What begins as a question about student use becomes a question about classroom design, institutional capacity, governance, or the structure of schooling itself.

Inside hierarchical systems of education, responsibility tends to be pushed downward. Systemic problems become teacher problems; instructional problems become student behaviors to monitor, regulate, or correct.

The work of visualization has not convinced me that the AI education debate is any less wicked than I thought. It has made me less certain, however, that wickedness requires us to remain trapped inside the same arguments.

Organisations are fairly good at rejecting obviously bad ideas. Individually attractive ideas that combine into something nobody intended are considerably more troublesome.

The company had built several systems capable of forming locally sensible interpretations of the same customer. Those systems had no shared interpretation of the customer as a whole. The customer was where the organisation finally came back together. What came back together looked absurd.
Shadow IT is technology the organisation does not fully know it has. Shadow agency is action the organisation does not fully know it has authorised. The consequences travel further.
The AI business case is incomplete until it accounts for the organisation AI creates around itself.

AI could make the organisation dramatically more productive. It could also create a new organisational role before anyone thought to design it: the person expected to reconstruct what distributed intelligence had done, reconcile competing consequences, explain the result, repair the relationships and remain accountable for the whole.

t: Teaching Trade-offs Are Hard to Observe

My student teacher has been doing none of these on purpose. What she's been doing looks like separation by space - tight in 3rd, loose in 4th - but it isn't a strategy. It's a reaction.

t: Research Bite #74: Digital Amnesia: The Aftermath of a Screenshot
q: Photography is one of the most common uses of a smartphone, and earlier work has shown that images we capture are remembered worse than images we simply look at. This study asked whether that cost buys us anything in return.

Screenshotting produced a large, consistent memory cost in every experiment. The predicted benefits did not appear: no better memory for where information came from, no improvement on a demanding maths task, and no boost to learning the material that came next.

But as we see in this experiment, students captured images on their own phones, in a task that took a second and involved no fiddling with unfamiliar equipment, and still remembered them substantially worse than images they only looked at.

The authors are explicit that their findings apply to material that is captured and then never revisited, which describes most of what sits in a camera roll. If students do photograph something, make the return trip part of the instruction.

Participants screenshotted material while genuinely engaged in a task about art, and still lost the detail. The feeling that something is safely stored is not a reliable signal that it has been learned.
Overall, these findings suggest that screenshotting imposes considerable memory costs without offering compensatory benefits.

When organisations reward outcomes alone, they risk undervaluing people doing excellent work in difficult circumstances. Metrics tell us something, but never the whole story.

That would actually be a major mistake. We know from the broader research literature that the spacing effect does work. This leads two possibilities: there is something about Bob's context that is so unique that it overturns decades of research on learning and memory; or the experiment was flawed, leading to a false negative.

The problems are exacerbated by the fact that most teachers are not experts in research methodology and statistics, and may lack experience, too. That is before we consider issues about research ethics, which are also riskier with inexperienced researchers.

So, I'm perfectly happy for all educators to engage in action research. I'd just warn against reading too much into findings - at least while one's understanding of methodology is still developing.

t: Prisoner's Dilemma: The Game Every Cross-Team Project Is Secretly Playing
q: Most teams call this a communication problem, or a trust problem, but what's really running it under the hood is the Prisoner's Dilemma.

The key insight of the Prisoner's Dilemma is this: when people make rational, self-protective decisions independently, they can add up to be the worse outcome for both parties than if they had simply trusted each other.

Both teams defect: both the teams build workarounds and diverge from the original spec, and when they finally meet, they find their implementations poles apart. This is the worst outcome because it requires the maximum rework.

As a leader who has visibility into both teams, and power to influence their goals and priorities, you can change how often the teams meet and coordinate. You can also set processes that catch defections or silos that lead to them in the first place.

One-shot games are harder to fix as they only involve "one" shot at the coordination or project. This is where the rational choice is typically deflection. Repeated games are those where the same teams work together again, and cooperation becomes the more rational choice.

Pay attention to the dynamics in the team - how they commit, how they coordinate with other teams, do they follow the agreed specs and terms, etc. Don't just assume that 'motivating' the team will be enough for them to build trust with each other.

t: Does Memory Make You... You?
q: When researchers, for instance, compared people's memories of major events, such as the September 11 terrorist attacks, they regularly found that participants' recollections, of which they were completely convinced, were often inconsistent with reality...or even with their own earlier accounts.

In many instances, they were only able to make sense of their own individual experiences after discussing the events with their comrades-in-arms, allowing them to place what had happened into a broader context. This, however, could also result in memory conformity, where the memories merge...a phenomenon known as the co-witness effect.

This was something the ancients knew all too well. Memory was a cornerstone of education, enshrined in religion, ritual, as well as everyday life. The Pythagoreans, for example, cultivated memory through daily discipline.
They were expected to review each day's words and deeds every morning and evening, while also committing their master's teachings to memory before they were ever written down.

You then decide upon a specific path through that place before assigning whatever needs memorizing to its different locations. The result is that you simply take your mental walk to remember each item or topic as you go.
We tend to shun rote learning, recalling (ironically) our painful experiences with multiplication tables, and so often view the practice as a form of torture, something that stifles our creativity...
At its most extreme, characters such as Leonard in Christopher Nolan's Memento demonstrate that without the ability to form new memories, life as we know it becomes almost impossible.

t: Classical Education Has a Machiavelli Problem
q: This essay is ultimately interested in whether or not the figure of Machiavelli can serve as a fitting exemplum and auctor for the project of contemporary classical education, but before addressing that matter directly, it is necessary to say a bit more about classical education and exempla in general.

To be clear, I do not object to teaching Machiavelli in classical education. This revolutionary and influential figure must be in curricula. However, influence and novelty do not equal the sapience, virtue, or artistic excellence requisite for a figure to serve as a fitting exemplum.

With revolutionary intent, Machiavelli boldly but wrongly redefines excellence (virtù) to include attributes like cruelty, violence, and victory rather than the excellences of the cardinal virtues as understood by Aristotle and Cicero. He subverts Christianity and makes the theological virtues into weaknesses.

Rather than explicitly offer Machiavelli as an exemplum, Freeman - without credit to the Italian - admires and wishes to inculcate a Machiavellian virtù. The result is a canon of thugs (with at least Jesus and Socrates dubiously canonized).

The Machiavellian frame that Olsen deploys suggests a problematic conflation of ambition for victory (gratification, fame, "greatness") and ambition for virtue (and virtuous achievement), and lacks the resources to distinguish between a settled affection of holy ambition and its counterfeit.

As we begin a new school year, may classical and liberal educators foreswear Machiavelli and rediscover and employ with honesty and piety those examples who actually capture the beauty of our noble activity.

t: Choosing Your Wife Everyday
q: Marriage is not choosing your wife. It's choosing your wife every day. By marrying your wife, you made an active choice. But you must keep making that same active choice every day for the rest of your life.
Yet your wife chose you before you gained all of this attractiveness. She chose you based on your potential. She chose you based on faith.
So, if you are not actively choosing her every day, she is rational in feeling a bit insecure. Men leave the wives of their youth for younger models all of the time. It's a cliché.

Your wife wants you to get more attractive. That's what she expected when she married you all those years ago. She wants other women to see how attractive you are. She wants to brag about the husband she chose.

What your wife wants is for you to have lots of other options…and then choose her, no matter what. To choose her every day. To come home every day. To love her and cherish her, words still included in many vows.
She chose you when you were still a boy. Choose her after you have become a man.

t: Can the Theory of Instruction Design Perfect Teaching?
q: Becky's argument is that each of these choices is defensible with reference to the Theory, and therefore it is solely my experience and expertise that pushed me to make a different - arguably better - decision. It's with this claim that I disagree.

The cuboid is the special case. In a right prism, all faces are rectangles except for the base, or cross-section. Therefore, this is the only example where the base shape matches every other face in the cuboid.
Therefore, is it defensible to ask students calculating the volume of solids for the very first time, and in the very first examples, to execute a multi-atom chain? No, it isn't.

The only way to develop that particular concept is through example sequences that force the learner to discriminate between what information they need and what they do not need - in other words, examples where more (and sometimes less) information is presented than they actually need.
The conclusion is that the Theory of Instruction does not permit you to algorithmically derive the exact correct approach to logically faultless communication. I think that remains correct.
Overall, I think Becky is probably right in her conclusion, you cannot simply feed the theory of instruction to an algorithmic system and expect it to output perfect instructional design.

t: 386. Just Enough Hope to Keep You From Leaving
q: It means when someone is giving you just enough attention to keep you emotionally invested, but not enough for any actual commitment. It's not ghosting. Breadcrumbing is worse. The person doesn't disappear. Instead, they drop just enough crumbs of interest to keep you waiting.

Each crumb keeps you hopeful. Each crumb keeps you working harder. And, more importantly, each crumb keeps you from interviewing somewhere else. You're not wrong to feel strung along. You are being strung along.

You don't breadcrumb others because you want to hurt them. You breadcrumb them because you don't want to have the hard conversation. You don't want to tell them the reality that the promotion isn't going to happen.
You think you're being kind by leaving the door open. You're not. You're being a coward. With every conversation that strings them along, you're eroding trust.

If you can't deliver on something, don't hint at it. If a promotion isn't coming, say it. Tell them that the thing they really want isn't going to happen anytime soon. Be specific. Be honest. Be clear.

Your childhood can influence the way you parent without becoming the childhood your own children are destined to have.
If nobody apologised in your house when you were growing up, where were you supposed to learn how to apologise to a child? Telling ourselves what we won't do can only take us so far.

t: Writing Is Thinking, Part I
q: Most of the time I understand something because I can feel the general shape of the idea in my mind. But when I try to write it down, I discover that the idea is incomplete.
Writing is more than a way to communicate a finished thought. It's one of the best ways we discover what we think.
If you begin criticizing every sentence before you have given yourself a chance to explore the idea, you may prevent yourself from discovering what you actually think.

Writing is useful because it gives you a place for your thoughts to be sorted out, which makes it easier to visually organize them. Your first explanation isn't going to be perfect, but that's okay because it's only for your eyes anyway.
This matters even more in the age of artificial intelligence because AI did not create passive learning. It made polished-looking passivity easier to produce.
My notebook, rough draft, or unfinished explanation gives AI something meaningful to respond to.
Writing is not only what happens after thinking. Writing is one of the places where thinking happens.

t: Why Did We Stop Building Beautiful Schools?
q: Writing in the first century BC, Vitruvius required three qualities of every public building: "All these should possess strength, utility, and beauty." A school that is merely strong and useful is still only two-thirds of a building.

At places such as Oxford, Cambridge, Paris, Bologna, and Salamanca, learning took place within a world of chapels, halls, libraries, cloisters, courtyards, gardens, and colleges. The student moved through spaces that continually reminded him that education belonged to something larger than the accumulation of useful information.
Every time a student walks past a really urgent, expressive piece of architecture that belongs to his college, it can help reassure him that he does have that mind, does have that soul.
The problem came when the underlying philosophy was reduced to a formula. Flat roof. Long corridor. Repeated windows. Cheap materials. Minimal decoration. Large parking area. Build another one.

The modern materials will produce a building which has all sorts of advantages, particularly cost, but they will last for only a few decades. A school that will be tired in thirty years cannot teach permanence.
A beautiful school tells a child that the work taking place inside deserves a worthy setting. It tells him that generations came before him and generations will follow.

We assess individual cognition in silence and call collaboration cheating. We've built an entire evaluative apparatus around the one axis machines have now comprehensively taken, while treating the axis where humans might still have something as misconduct.

t: Three Ways to Redesign an AI-Vulnerable Assessment
q: Tasks that are easily offloadable, and stay with me here, will be easily offloaded by our students. In fact, the best way to ensure students miss out on crucial learning and formation is by operating under the assumption that our assessment tasks are still fit for purpose in an AI world.
I remember the first time I saw a student do a two-week task in a single day. I was gutted.
In an AI world, assessment should be a treasure hunt, not a witch hunt. It's about encouraging learning, not prosecuting cheating.
A $20 essay with a $2 reflection isn't proof that a student has outsourced to AI, but it does show us that the formation we had hoped for perhaps hasn't taken place.
And if there is nothing more than a few tumbleweeds for the first few steps and then a perfect, typo-free assessment is submitted, that's a good time to have a conversation with the learner.
Now that students can complete work in less time with less engagement than ever before, we need to be wise about how we assess student knowledge and skill.

t: The Power of Friday Night Lights: What School Redesign Can Learn From the Power of Community and Culture
q: Sometimes we assume that if we simply create more compelling learning opportunities, people will choose them. But that underestimates the power of culture and community.

To be clear, Friday Night Lights isn't really about football. It's about everything surrounding it. The game. The student section. The band. The jerseys at school on Friday. The homecoming dance. And even the drama.

Humans are social creatures. For most of human history, our survival depended on being part of a group. We watch what other people do. We learn the norms of our communities. Over time, those repeated experiences become culture.

If we believe all young people need opportunities to develop agency, judgment, communication, collaboration, creativity, adaptability, and the other durable skills required for life, work, and citizenship, these experiences cannot be limited to those who choose a specialized program or different school models.
They could still show up Friday night. They could eat lunch with their friends, share traditions, play sports together, perform in the same theater, and contribute to the same community.
The goal isn't to get rid of Friday Night Lights. The goal is to preserve what communities value while building a version of school worth showing up for on Monday morning, too.

t: The Gentleman and the Power of Responsibility
q: Blame gives you the illusion of moral high ground. It removes the burden of effort and accountability. It soothes one's ego by saying, "This isn't my fault." However, in the process, blame steals your power to improve your circumstances.

Agency is the belief and the ability to shape your future through your choices. It is the recognition that your decisions matter, that your habits compound, and that your character is revealed in what you choose to do each day.
In combat and in life, Jocko observed that the best leaders never make excuses. They own the mission entirely. "There are no bad teams, only bad leaders," he wrote.

A hard truth is that no mentor, boss, spouse, or government program can live your life for you. A gentleman embraces this fact. He knows that if something is going to happen, it's up to him to make it happen.

Victimhood is a character flaw that impairs one's ability to excel in life. It's a worldview that convinces you that nothing is your fault, and therefore nothing can be changed. This mindset is a slow death. It breeds bitterness and envy.

Taking responsibility means choosing discipline over indulgence. It means showing up on time, paying your debts, and working when you don't feel like it. It means keeping promises, especially to yourself.

t: Second-Hand Knowledge
q: In practice, almost everything a non-specialist believes about science has arrived second-hand. So the brain misconception is not an isolated accident. It is what often happens to research once it leaves the circle of people equipped to read it in its original form.

A specific, hard-won finding about disconnected hemispheres became a claim about everyone: that each of us is ruled by one side, the logical left or the creative right. From there it hardened into a personality type, repeated in magazines, printed on classroom worksheets and sold in workshops.
Underneath these examples sits an uncomfortable asymmetry. A wrong idea that is simple and memorable travels further than a correct one buried in qualification.

It can produce a summary that reads beautifully and carries every mark of confidence whether or not it is correct, in the same way the personality quiz did, only generated in seconds and at a scale no magazine ever managed.

t: Organizations That Must Look for Talent From the Outside
q: While circumstances can occur that dash well-laid plans, having to hire an outside CEO is a signal that developing the leadership pipeline has been a low priority or ignored over a long period of time.

What begins as a minor shortfall in succession planning can, within a decade, become a full-blown crisis. This forces boards and decision-makers into rushed, high-stakes external searches at the exact moments when stability and institutional knowledge matter most.

That means dedicating real resources to stretch assignments, mentorship, honest performance feedback, and structured coaching. Leadership capability, like any other organizational asset, must be built deliberately and continuously.

Organizations that excel at leadership development also become magnets for talent. Those that neglect the work of talent development find themselves at the mercy of the external marketplace, where they must pay a premium for talent they could have grown themselves.

Given that roughly 40 percent of all externally hired senior leaders fail or materially underperform within the first 18-24 months, creating a strong talent pipeline is not just a leadership imperative. It is a business imperative.

t: How to Fix Your Focus in One Day

I sort them into 4 categories: Today. This Week. Scheduled / Waiting. Someday. I triage my inbox 2-3 times a day. So by the end of the day it should nearly be empty.

Singularity of focus is one of the greatest predictors of your success. Because to do great things, we must do fewer things.

t: How Bad Ideas Can Destroy You
q: But you'd be wrong if you thought that Dostoevsky was only concerned with action. In fact, he was just as concerned with the ways that ideas, and especially false ideas, can lead to a person's destruction.

He's a philosopher and a truly brilliant writer, so much so that he writes essays on theology that confound even the learned monks and theologians of the local monastery. There's just one problem: Ivan is deeply nihilistic, too.
All I know is that there is suffering and that there are none guilty... I must have justice, or I will destroy myself.
I want to see with my own eyes the hind lie down with the lion and the victim rise up and embrace his murderer. I want to be there when everyone suddenly understands what it has all been for.

Ivan realizes that, if there is indeed no universal purpose, and everything is absurd, then there is surely no good reason to reject any action on fundamentally moral grounds. Instead, Ivan accepts total moral anti-realism: If God does not exist, anything must be permitted.
It is this principle that Dostoevsky finds most dangerous, and as we shall see, it makes Ivan's statement that he would "destroy himself" more prophetic than he realizes.

t: Does Checking for Attention Work?
q: High-frequency questions a teacher fires out at students, pretty much after every sentence of an explanation. The questions are designed for 100% of students to be able to answer successfully, provided they were paying attention.

We're confronted with a room full of children in which some are attentive, some pretending, some drifting, some lost, some trying hard but failing to track. Our problem is practical and immediate: how do we know whether every students is with me right now?

If I have attended to every part of your explanation, and to every question after every part of your explanation, will I have a better understanding of the whole explanation? That is not my experience of students in the classroom.

What I am very unlikely to be doing is paying attention to how the different parts of the explanation stick together. Too much has got in the way. I might never fail to repeat what my teacher has said. But the whole explanation is much less likely to cohere.
Your goal is not attention, your goal is learning. Attention is a proxy for learning and can actually get in the way of learning if you focus on the proxy itself.
But, I am not checking for attention. I am checking for understanding. My students, your students, will feel that difference.

t: A Tale of Two Bens: What Happens When We Decide a Child's Future at 14?
q: His dad was injured at work and had been out of work since Ben was 10 years old. To pay for food, school uniforms and the roof over his head, his mum was forced to work two jobs.

Moving this choice to the point before they get their GCSEs, never mind the fact they are only 13 or 14 when they do choose, is putting up walls that today, do not exist.

t: Why You Need a Lesson Observation Methodology
q: We all have established practices for lesson observations but we might not have a methodology.

...when untrained observers are asked to judge the quality of a lesson, there is likely to be only modest agreement among them. Worse still, even if they do agree that what they see is good practice, it often actually isn't.

School leaders are not typically formally trained in observing lessons. Some schools might put on in house observation training, but this can still simply magnify some of Coe's reasons for unreliability.

When we do not have a methodology, what gets noticed in a lesson depends on who is watching. Two observers in the same room will see different things, value different things and feed back different things.

Without a methodology that specifies what observers need to know and how they are trained, observation defaults to what is most visible; the pace of the lesson, whether students appear busy, whether the teacher seems confident.

A single observation by a single observer is not enough. Without multiple observations, multiple observers, agreed criteria, independent recording and a moderation process, the judgement is more likely to reflect the observer's preferences than the reality of teaching in the school.
Other professions don't leave high stakes judgements to individual impression and neither should we.

t: Closing Our Leadership Rings
q: No individual leader can possibly know the full reality of school life. And the more senior that leader is, the less likely it is that they can know the reality because truth doesn't rise to the top.
It is a fundamental job of a school leader to aim to close their rings between the reality of school life and what we imagine it to be.
Too often, people ask 'Any questions?'. While seemingly harmless, this phrase and how it is delivered is loaded with meaning.
If a leadership team all have a similar background and similar experiences, there is a very real risk that they are hampered from the outset in closing their leadership rings.
Making sense without giving sense risks leadership becoming an internal exercise only. Closing the rings requires us not just to understand reality, but to help others navigate it with us.

This is a relational act, not a command and control one. The goal is not to impose a fixed narrative or tell others what to think, but to stabilise meaning in times of disruption, to frame change without forcing it, and to provide clarity without the false promise of certainty.
Colleagues often look to leaders for certainty, especially during times of disruption. But offering false certainty can backfire.

After gathering feedback, sense giving closes the leadership rings by returning to the community with Here's what you told us, here's how we've interpreted it, and here's how it has shaped our decisions.

t: 5 Composure Habits for Experts Who Go Quiet When Someone Pushes Back
q: Your director cuts across you at minute nine. She says the approach worries her, and she says it in front of six people. Heat arrives in your chest before any thought does.
My first theory was courage, which turned out to be wrong. What they actually had was a slightly longer gap between the feeling and the response. That gap is the entire skill.
This quarter that costs you a recommendation. Over three years it becomes the thing people know about you, which is that you fold when pressed. Nobody says it out loud.

A person who does not flinch appears to have already considered the objection, whether or not they have. That inference happens automatically in the people watching, and it is why the same argument delivered without wobble gets treated as more thoroughly tested.

When someone challenges you, close your mouth and count to three. Not a dramatic pause. Three actual seconds while you look at them. It will feel like fifteen from the inside and like composure from the outside.
Then stop again. The temptation to add supporting detail is the failure mode. Detail after a challenge reads as bargaining.
The clean version is one sentence with a reason and no padding. "I can't take that on this month, I'd have to drop the migration work to do it." Then silence.
Mistake to avoid: the fake apology. "So sorry, I really wish I could" tells them the no is soft and worth pushing on. Say no once, plainly, and let it sit there.
When someone pushes back, look at them while they speak and while you answer. Dropping your eyes mid-sentence is read as concession before you have said anything.

t: The Version of Me You Won't Find on LinkedIn

t: The Staff Meeting Where Everyone Stopped Talking
q: I asked the staff whether the new dismissal procedure was working. It was a fair question and an easy one, the kind that used to get four hands up before I finished asking it. This time nobody spoke.

By early November I had three resignation letters all from teachers with six or more years in my building, all citing some version of personal or family reasons, all handed in without the conversation beforehand that used to precede a veteran teacher's decision to leave.
The pattern was there once I looked for it. Fewer questions each month. Fewer objections. A room that had gone from arguing with me to simply absorbing whatever I said.

Three separate times I made a call and explained it after the fact instead of before. Each time felt small on its own. Together, they taught forty adults that raising a hand had stopped being worth the effort.

t: Two Fights Before Labor Day
q: Two fights in eleven school days, before Labor Day even arrived. I told the superintendent both were unrelated. I was wrong about that before the ink dried on my own report.

Both fights happened during the same twelve-minute window, the unsupervised stretch between the first bell and when homeroom attendance officially started, a gap that had grown by six minutes when the district shifted the bus schedule in July and nobody adjusted staff duty assignments to match.

I pulled the duty schedule and mapped every adult's actual location during that window, not their assigned location, the actual one. Two duty posts had quietly gone unfilled since a retirement in the spring that nobody had backfilled on the schedule itself, only in the budget line.
I reassigned two teachers with open first-period preps to cover that window starting the next Monday. No fight has happened in that twelve-minute stretch since.

But behavior clusters around time and place before it clusters around cause. A school leader who checks the clock and the map before accepting the easy explanation catches structural gaps that a second, third, or fourth incident will otherwise reveal the hard way.

Research suggests colleagues who simply learn of or witness a teammate being recognized perceive greater organizational fairness and become more committed to their own success, even though the recognition wasn't directed at them.
