Since setbacks and failures weigh two to three times more heavily on morale than equivalent gains, customer success stories function as a counterweight, giving the team a steady flow of positivity to offset the inevitable frustrations of customer-facing work.
Giving the person involved the floor to describe the experience in their own words is a form of respect that reinforces their sense of ownership over the win.
When leaders make a habit of turning individual wins into shared stories, customer success becomes a renewable source of collective pride.

t: The Shared Enemy - Best Practices
q: 99.5% of megaprojects fail to meet their budget, schedule, and benefits targets. (Flyvbjerg)
Snowden and Flyvbjerg are intellectual allies with opposing approaches to project management. They diagnose the same symptoms and prescribe different cures.
Snowden argues that forcing things into order is exactly how systems fail, and Flyvbjerg is trying to turn the unordered into the ordered.

Dave Snowden, on the other hand, warns against looking at a few successful companies, finding something they all do, and then saying, "Do this, and you will succeed." He says this mixes up things that happen together (correlation) with things that actually cause results (causation).

Know the type of project you have: Don't mistake a complex project for a complicated one. They operate differently and should be managed differently. Complicated is sense first. Complex is probe first.
For example, Healthcare.gov was actually a complex project but wasn't executed that way... They brought in a small team to probe, sense, and respond in real-time and it worked.
Pairing the outside view (Flyvbjerg) with the emergent view (Snowden) we can stop forcing a square peg into a round hole. Doing this we learn to slow down to speed up.

t: The Screenish Inquisition: The Newest Excuse Not to Reform Education
q: We handed it to the kids with no instruction, and then acted betrayed when they used it as a slot machine.
The word for the move is screenwashing: washing your hands of a systemic problem by pointing at a screen.

The largest analysis of the screen-time literature, 350,000 adolescents across three datasets, found that digital technology use explains at most 0.4 percent of the variation in well-being, roughly the same association as eating potatoes.

The first nationally representative study of school phone bans, from the University of Birmingham across 30 English schools, found no difference in well-being, sleep, or attainment between restrictive and permissive schools.

And PISA 2022 found that students who used devices for up to an hour a day of learning in school scored 14 points higher in math than those who used none, while students distracted by classmates' devices scored 15 points lower.
The phone is in use a median of 43 minutes a school day. The school day runs roughly 400. If the phone is stealing 43 minutes, who is responsible for the other 357?
Teachers earned 26.9 percent less per week in 2024 than similarly educated professionals, the widest gap in three decades of tracking. A ban is cheaper than a raise.
Ban the phones if you must. Then do the work. Teach the tools. Ask the kids. Pay the adults. Fund the ones who are falling behind.

t: The Science of Education
q: The trouble begins when we confuse the use of science in education with the direct application of individual research results to education. Those aren't the same thing.
Scientific knowledge grows as a connected structure, an organism, rather than as a heap of individually impressive studies, a clump of cells.
No genuine science is formed by isolated conclusions, however exact the measurements or impeccable the technique by which those conclusions were reached.

It is not the capable engineer who treats scientific findings as imposing upon him a certain course which is to be rigidly adhered to: it is the third or fourth-rate man who adopts this course. Even more, it is the unskilled day laborer who follows it.

Understanding a memory phenomenon during an experiment and deciding how that understanding should be used when teaching fractions, historical causation, reading, or electrical circuits are different intellectual problems.
Dewey thought classroom teachers should contribute to the development of educational knowledge because they're in direct contact with the phenomena the science is trying so hard to understand.
It's not a conveyor belt running from laboratory to classroom, but a two-way street that travels in both directions with science informing practice and practice informing science.

t: The Real Story in Maine
q: That was our fault. Not the devices. Ours. We led with platforms instead of purpose. We bought first and asked pedagogical questions later.

He admits, twice, that the data proves nothing. "Is this proof that laptops harmed learning? Of course not." ... Then he waves all of that away in a single paragraph and lets the correlation do the persuading anyway. That's not analysis. That's a chart with a vibe.

Massachusetts passed the Education Reform Act in 1993, massive funding increases, curriculum frameworks, MCAS accountability, a full decade before MLTI existed. Its rise to the top of NAEP is one of the most studied policy stories in American education, and laptops have nothing to do with it.

The research literature he references, including the Zheng meta-analysis he links, finds 1:1 programs produce small positive effects, around +0.12 to +0.16. Small. Positive. Not transformational, and not harmful.

The first study of its kind, the SMART Schools study out of the University of Birmingham, published in The Lancet Regional Health, Europe (2025), compared 1,227 students across 30 schools and found no difference in mental wellbeing, anxiety, depression, sleep, physical activity, or academic attainment between schools that ban phones and schools that don't.
Conflating a consumer smartphone loaded with TikTok and a managed school device running a writing workshop is either careless or deliberate. Neither is good research.
They're doing the harder, quieter work: recalibrating, centering technology intentionally, asking "why this tool, for this learning, right now?" That's the work. It always was.

t: The Five Worst Education Cliches
q: As soon as certain topics are raised, the concrete melts into the abstract and no one seems able to think of turns of speech that are not hackneyed: prose consists less and less of words chosen for the sake of their meaning, and more and more of phrases tacked together like the sections of a prefabricated henhouse.

Public discourse involving those who have been elected to office, and are subject to public scrutiny, is dismissed as a game by those who would see less democracy in education and more bureaucratic control by unaccountable vested interests.
The greatest irony here is that, in many respects, the alternatives to exams might seem more like factory work. Anyone involved in the "manufacture" of coursework can see that.

If you want education to go beyond the academic, into therapy, social work, entertainment, preaching and parenting, then this cliche can be used to suggest all aspects of a child's life fall in the domain of teachers.

Suddenly, those who support equal rights and equal entitlements for all children are expected to explain why they are ignoring differences between children, while those who support inequality are no longer expected to demonstrate that the differences they perceive justify different and/or unequal treatment.
If you feel inclined to use any of these phrases in education discussion, I challenge you to try to express the same idea in your own words.

t: Students Should Only Use AI for Things They Already Know How to Do Well
q: Students should only use AI for things that they already know how to do well.
Learning is a product of engaging in mental work, and students may use AI to replace that mental work and hence, not to learn.

No one wants to read the papers they write, and the math problems they solve have no practical value. Teachers have them do these tasks because they provide practice in cognitive abilities that we think matter.
For many educators, writing papers was the only tool we had to ensure that students engage these cognitive processes. AI took that tool from us, and we don't know of a good replacement.
Artificial Intelligence tools should not substitute for tasks wherein students would benefit from doing the mental work themselves.
The novice doesn't know enough to ask good questions. He will give the AI system a vague prompt about the goal of the exercise whereupon AI will sharpen it for the user.

We've all heard "They're going to have to learn to use AI." But I think that slogan applies to how students will use AI at home and in the workforce, where the product is the thing. For students, learning is the thing.

t: Start Strong: Five Classroom Foundations That Pay Off All Year
q: A strong start is the deliberate, explicit teaching of five foundational routines that help make your classroom run like clockwork.
A new class that spends September unsure of what to do spends the rest of the year paying that tax in lost attention and disrupted learning.
Working memory is limited, and it doesn't distinguish between "productive thinking about your lesson" and "working out where to sit, whether it's safe to answer, and what happens if I get this wrong.
A class that doesn't yet trust the routines, doesn't know whether participation is safe, and can't predict what's coming next is a class whose motivation system is quietly voting to disengage.
A success rate of 80 percent shows that students are learning the material, and it also shows that the students are challenged." — Barak Rosenshine, Principles of Instruction (2012)
A routine taught once in September and never revisited decays exactly the way any other unpractised skill does.

An attention signal is far less useful without an entry routine that's already secured a calm start. Paired talk only works if early tasks have already built enough confidence that students have something worth saying to a partner.
Get these five running by the end of the first fortnight, and you've removed five recurring taxes on attention that would otherwise be quietly charged every lesson until July.

t: Paige Pullen on "The Canon" and Special Education
a: John Lloyd and Paige C. Pullen
q: Our field has five decades of reading research and no shared standard, which is how "evidence-based" ends up stamped on two practices that contradict each other. In the area of literacy, educators are data-rich and synthesis-poor.
A great deal of what we now call the science of reading was learned from children who struggled to read.
Direct Instruction was built and tested with the children the system was failing, and it became a mainstay of special education before the wider field rediscovered it.
A student who is behind is usually the student we ask to hold the most at once, because we are trying to make up ground. Working memory does not grant an exception for urgency.
I have literally seen districts require three different programs for different tiers of instruction, rather than intensifying the instruction through pacing, group size, duration, and frequency.
An IEP has to be determined by data and delivered in the least restrictive environment, and that is not aspiration; it is the law and the daily practice.
Adams told us in 1990 what children need to learn about print. We are still arguing about it in 2026. The science settled; the field never did.

t: Ohio's Implementation of the Science of Reading
q: Approximately half of American adults read at a sixth-grade level or below, according to the Barbara Bush Foundation.
In Ohio, 38 percent of fourth graders and 31 percent of eighth graders scored "below basic" on the most recent National Assessment of Educational Progress.
Ohio unfortunately gutted the retention requirement: state lawmakers in 2023 weakened the guarantee's retention provision by allowing schools to promote struggling students based on parental request.

In 2024-25, 98 percent of third graders were promoted despite a statewide third grade reading proficiency rate of just 61 percent. Of the grade-promoted students, 21,658 students advanced to fourth grade through the parental loophole.

By the end of 2025, a large majority of Ohio classroom teachers, reading specialists, and administrators, more than 115,000 educators in all, completed an introductory professional development (PD) course in the science of reading.
Thirty-eight out of 48 programs were deemed in full or partial alignment but 10 failed the audit, including Ohio University and Ohio State University.
Literacy has the power to change lives. It can unlock further education and rewarding careers. It opens minds to new ideas and ways of thinking.

t: Nixon-Era Laws, Harry Potter, and the Russian Email That Skeeved Me Out
q: Every time an IT department skuttles a software request without explanation, what's happening is that you're actually staring at a giant, toothy legal machine grinding away beneath our classrooms.
Legally, FERPA states data is not de-identified if a reasonable person in the school community could figure out who wrote it. Modern machine learning shatters that standard without flinching.
Eight people raised their hands and positively identified my son by name. De-identified does not stop something from being easily re-identified, especially with the power of AI behind the task.
When a splash page screams "FERPA Compliant," laugh. FERPA binds educational institutions. It literally cannot bind a private software vendor.

By using targeted extraction prompts, researchers pulled over 90 percent of entire copyrighted books like Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone word for word, while image diffusion models have been caught faithfully reconstructing private, copyrighted photos directly from their training sets.
They are likely doing the grueling, unglamorous work of standing between your students and a multi-billion-dollar data extraction engine that views classroom work as free training material.
In this new era, protecting student privacy is no longer just an IT headache. It is classroom management. It is digital ethics.

t: How to Live Life Like Frieren: An Anime About the Human Condition
q: At its heart, Frieren is a story about learning to notice a human life before it disappears.
Why didn't I try to get to know him better?" The tragedy was not that Frieren lacked time. She had more time than almost anyone. The tragedy was that she assumed time would always remain available.
Frieren overlooks life because she believes she has endless time. We overlook it because we believe we never have enough.

In a well-known study, participants remembered information better when they were highly curious about the answer. Even more interestingly, heightened curiosity also improved memory for unrelated information encountered along the way.
These scenes are not filler. They are the substance of the relationships.
Across four studies, people underestimated how interesting and pleasurable it would be to revisit records of their everyday lives.
Life is longer than the next deadline, and much shorter than we think.

t: Founder Mode Is the Wrong Answer to the AI Moment
q: Kelly's take: "AI is becoming a very expensive way to realize how poorly designed our workplaces were in the first place.
Most reward systems still pay you for the number of humans you manage rather than the outcomes you generate, which is why every reorg turns into a headcount negotiation.

Instead, most AI transformation to date is mostly just cutting: leave the function as-is, reduce by 20% and the survivors have to adopt AI to deliver against the old output goals. No changes to the machine itself, just a different fuel mix.
In a startup of 10 people, you can have a hive mind; as you scale to 30, founder mode is leadership. At thirty thousand, it's cosplay.

James Daunt pushed power out of HQ and gave book buying decisions back to store managers: what to stock, how to shelve it, and what goes on the front table... It worked. The center got smaller, and they opened 50 stores last year, back near their all-time high.
Stanford's Digital Economy Lab finds employment for 22-to-25-year-olds in AI-exposed occupations runs about 19% below the comparison with peers in less-exposed jobs, up from 15% a year ago.

What people are desperate for right now is a sense of steadiness. No matter what's coming at us, this is who I am, this is how I show up every day, and this is the value we're going to create together.
Only 13% of AI users feel rewarded for reinventing work if there's a short term hit and 45% say it's safer to just focus on hitting today's number.

t: For Us, There's Only War
q: I also dream of something simpler: my wife, my children, some animals, and a peaceful life in the mountains, away from the chaos and toxicity of our times.

And as much as it pains me to accept it, my dream is naive and cowardly, for to live it would be to abandon the fight and run away into hiding, leaving behind all those souls who are lost and hurting.

We are the weak men amidst the hard times. And it will stay that way until someone has the guts to lead the charge and bring about the next phase of this never-ending cycle. Someone has to do it. Might as well be us.

I accept the possibility that I won't get to see the end of this war. All I can hope for is that before my death comes, I will have done some good, and I will have fought bravely and honorably, for a cause greater than my own selfish goals and dreams.

For us, there might be only war. Fifty years of disappointments, fifty years of pain, fifty years of necessary sacrifice to expose the horrors that lurk beneath the surface of this putrid and corrupted social fabric.
But not us. Not now. Not here. Not today. Our duty is to fight. If we are to give our children the freedom we strive for, we can't cowardly retreat and abandon the fight.

t: Education's Ambulance-at-the-Bottom Problem
q: There's an old adage that it's better to build a sturdy fence at the top of a cliff than station an ambulance at the bottom.
Schools aren't held accountable for reading and math outcomes until the end of third grade, even though many of the conditions that shape student success take hold well before then.
By the time a student has misbehaved himself into suspension, expulsion, or involvement with law enforcement, the school is often dealing with behavior that has escalated over months or even years.

A student who learns to read well in the early grades may never need tutoring, but there is no obvious crisis to point to as evidence that the early instruction worked... As Mitch Daniels often says, "Dogs don't bark at parked cars.
My former boss, Tony Bennett, often talked about how the traditional system is organized around adult comfort rather than what's best for children.
The point isn't that every problem can be headed off. Sometimes the ambulance is exactly what's needed. Tier II and Tier III supports matter.
The alternative is to keep asking schools to solve problems after they've become intractable.

t: Education as a Space Inbetween
q: My English teacher had come to ask why I had not returned to school. ... I remember the fear that settled almost instantly in the pit of my stomach. Not because I had been found... but because I knew the volatility of the man standing on the other side of the front door.

I have never questioned that my English teacher changed the course of my life. Had she not stood on that doorstep on a September evening, I suspect my life would have followed an entirely different trajectory.

Teachers expected me to think. They expected me to read beyond the set text, to wrestle with ideas, to argue a point and support it with evidence. They assumed that university was a possibility long before I believed it was.
Education did not reduce the complexity of my life. It temporarily reduced what was being asked of me within it.
My task was not to organise the future, solve every problem or continually prove my competence. My task was to learn.
At certain moments in a life, education can become an environment that temporarily carries more than the individual can. Not permanently and not as an escape from responsibility, but long enough.

I think I returned because, at several crucial moments, learning offered me a way of inhabiting the world differently. It allowed me, for a while, to step out of the role I had been carrying and into one where growth itself was enough.

t: Education Gadfly Weekly: Charter Schools, Ambulance-at-the-Bottom, and Ohio Science of Reading
q: Charter schools remain one of the clearest successes of the education reform era, but the rise of vouchers and education savings accounts is changing the competitive landscape. If policymakers want charters to remain a strong public option, they will need to reduce needless regulation and give them room to compete.

Schools too often wait until students are already struggling before they respond, whether in reading, math, behavior, or foreign language instruction. A better approach would ask what needs to happen earlier, and what supports schools need before problems become harder and more expensive to solve.

Fordham's latest report documents the significant work Ohio has undertaken to implement science of reading reforms. But the job isn't done, and the state will need sustained leadership, accountability, and attention to vocabulary and background knowledge if its policies are to translate into higher reading achievement.

New York City tried to broaden school accountability by adding qualitative reviews of instruction, school culture, and improvement systems. New research finds that these reviews may offer useful signals about school quality but produced little evidence of sustained gains in student outcomes on their own.
The Emerging Education Policy Scholars (EEPS) program seeks to counter the long-standing, well-documented divide between research and policy in education.

t: Can Charter Schools Survive Universal School Choice? https://fordhaminstitute.org/national/commentary/can-charter-schools-survive-universal-school-choice
q: The charter sector remains one of the few reforms of that period that (just about) everyone agrees was a success. They're popular, they boast real academic advantages over traditional public schools, especially for poor kids, and, through competitive effects, they even improve the outcomes of students in those nearby traditional public schools.
Charter schools are now "forced to compete against nimble, less-regulated ESA-funded providers while operating under heavier compliance and resource constraints than traditional districts are.

In Arizona, where the universal ESA has been in place the longest, "nearly half of leaders indicated that students had already left their schools to use ESA funds," with reported withdrawals ranging from a single student to dozens or even hundreds in larger schools.

Most of them emphasized that they're more interested in reforming charter schools to allow them to better compete with ESAs than to abandon the market altogether, noting that charter schools maintain strong reputations and that they provide "appropriate governance, accountability, and oversight.

A strong education marketplace requires many options, public, private, and charter. Moreover, if the sector dies with a whimper, those within it suggest that it will come through overregulation, not its own failures.
To do otherwise is to risk letting one of the primary successes of the bipartisan education reform movement become just another failure.

t: Build the Comment Bank Now, or Type the Same Note Forty Times in October
q: Fourth hour of grading. Assignment thirty-one. You type "your thesis is a topic, not an argument" for the twenty-fifth time, except by now it comes out as "unclear thesis, see me.
The comments we repeat most are the ones that matter most. We repeat them because the mistake is universal in our course. They also degrade fastest under fatigue.
Write each one well, one time, while you're calm and not staring down a stack. Then pull from that bank instead of retyping it at 11pm.
Every banked comment gets one line specific to that student before it goes out. The banked part carries the teaching. The one custom line makes a student feel like a person read their work.
Ten seconds instead of four minutes. The student gets the calm August version of your thinking, not the paper-thirty-one version.

You finish at midnight and you know the last ten students got less than the first ten. In the other, you paste, you add one line about paragraph three, and you're done in half the time. Every student gets the version you wrote when you were thinking clearly.

t: Build or Buy AI Tools: Why Renting Capability Backfires
q: The company owns licenses, yet the vendor owns the practical knowledge. That arrangement may deliver a tool. It rarely creates internal AI capability.
Buying an AI tool solves a defined problem at a specific moment. Building capability changes how the organization responds to problems for years.

The claims processor knows which parts of a file require judgment. The customer-service representative knows which questions waste the most time. The HR coordinator knows where onboarding repeatedly breaks down.
In a study of 5,179 customer-support agents, access to an AI assistant increased productivity by 14 percent on average, with much larger gains among less-experienced workers.
Citizen builders should not quietly construct systems that approve loans, make medical recommendations, determine employment outcomes, or bypass established controls.

Do not ask only, "Which AI system should we buy?" Ask, "What must our people learn to build, improve, and govern for themselves?" Vendors can supply technology. Consultants can accelerate the journey. Neither should own your organization's ability to innovate.

t: A Mother's Letter to Her Son on the Day He Leaves Home
q: Exactly 17 years, 2 weeks, and 1 day after I brought you home from the midwifery clinic in Toronto, a screaming, red-faced, shrivelled little human, we have reached the end of your childhood.
Then you were my baby. Now you are my child." The next part was left unsaid, but I can hear it in my head. "Eventually, you will be a man.
Live your life; don't perform it. It's tempting to do things for an online audience, and even to select activities based on their potential appeal for social media posts, but resist that urge.
Err on the side of compassion. You never know what a person is dealing with, what burdens they might be carrying, what sort of awful day they may have had.
Mary Oliver wrote, "To pay attention, this is our endless and proper work." Do that. Do it for yourself, do it for others. Give them the gift of your full attention.
Books will make you smarter than anything; they will expose you to challenging new ideas that require you to sit with your thoughts and contemplate the world, as humans have done for millennia.

I've revelled in raising you for 17 years, but now I have to let you go, pretty much as far away as it's physically possible to go! I will miss you so much, but seeing how excited you are to venture out into the world makes it easier to say goodbye.

t: What If We Stopped Starting Over
q: Every discipline that improves does it the same way. You keep what works, you isolate the part that doesn't, and you revise that part. NASA engineers do not throw out entire Mars rovers. They observe, they analyze, they figure out which component failed, and they fix that component.

For whatever reason, education does not work this way. Education throws the whole thing out and starts from scratch. Or rather, it pretends to start from scratch while actually grabbing onto the same thing that didn't work eight years ago.

For example, this 2007 study on teachers' perceptions of the basal program Open Court could easily be swapped out for 2025 teacher rhetoric regarding popular basals of today, such as Into Reading and Wonders.

Teachers felt Open Court's rapid instructional pace and lack of meaningful interaction led students to tune out. Teachers also noted that the program's guidance for differentiating instruction for English learners was not helpful in practice.

What students need instead is deep, multi-year teacher training that leaves teachers able to teach reading with any program, or with none. Scripted programs are great for teachers who are still learning on their path to mastery. But they are a crutch, and eventually every teacher should be able to run without them.
Fidelity to best practice will always win over fidelity to any box.

t: What I Think Could Be Challenging This School Year and How I Want to Respond
q: In a class of 25-28 students, if you ask me how Albert is doing? 100% of the time, I have a genuine answer I can give you. In a class of 30-33 students, however, if you ask me about Albert? I cannot guarantee that I'll have a genuine answer every single class period.

I think this instinct is understandable but also at least partially incorrect. In particular, I believe that if I go into the school year with a behavior management lens, then it will be self-fulfilling prophecy as far as the culture of the classroom that emerges in response.

To name some other challenges, all of which feel as if they are increasing: increased guidance from the district around writing assessments, increased embedding of AI tools into actual writing platforms that students use, increased norming of AI-generated feedback amongst teachers.

As Jennifer Haber wrote, before we can help students regulate, we have to notice when we're becoming dysregulated ourselves. This means being reflective not just on what I'm doing as a teacher but even more so how I'm doing.
My fear essentially is this: too many adults, including too many adults working in public schools, have decided that public schools aren't good enough for their own children.
There are consequences for not telling and sharing the good stories about what is happening in our schools, and I fear that we're only starting to see those consequences.

t: The Power Shift: Why Top-Down Authority Doesn't Work Anymore
q: Authority is attached to your role and your responsibilities, not your title or your confidence level on a given day.
When someone keeps overriding your decisions, the fix is usually clarity, not conflict. Share your thinking, not just your conclusion.
Being 'too nice' is frequently a symptom of not trusting your own authority.

Barbara tells a story about a team member who owned the leadership meeting agenda on paper but kept getting steamrolled by a supervisor who needed to feel like the expert. The fix wasn't a bigger title or a tougher tone. It was sending her thinking along with her draft, so there was nothing left to override.

Heather tells a story from her own Thanksgiving table, where a guest tried to rewrite the whole menu over a dietary restriction, and the host quietly reclaimed her authority by handling it one on one instead of letting the group weigh in.

t: The Greatest Enemy
q: It turns out that demanding relationships are demanding and we are out of practice. So when offered the choice between it and a substitution, some cheap plastic, Chinese brand knock off, it's quite tempting to go with the knock off.

Consider, the archetypes of the rugged individual, the resourceful guy who doesn't need anyone, the man who just wants to be left alone, the parents dedicated to their own set of rules and pursuits, or the online mutuals who have a deep connection to their esoteric knowledge.
Culturally, we hold this idea of radical individualism so sacred that there's essentially no relationship which can't be justly severed if it's not in service to being authentically ourselves.

When the world is full of radical individuals, as it is now, institutions themselves lose the relational context to form anyone. All that's left to do is for mass institutions to herd us about, like the powerless cattle we are.
I believe I can have my cake and eat it too. That I can retain almost all of the amazing benefits of modern life while also enjoying the fruits of demanding family and communal relationships.
As good as formative relationships sound to the ear, it comes with the burden of compromise, inconvenience, and deference.

t: The 5 Mental Skills That Matter More Than Motivation
q: A person can feel deeply inspired and still be unable to manage distraction, tolerate discomfort, think clearly under pressure, or control an emotional reaction. Another person may feel completely unmotivated and still move through the day with discipline because they have developed something more reliable than enthusiasm.

Whatever repeatedly receives your attention begins to feel important, whether it deserves that importance or not. If you constantly attend to comparison, you will feel behind. If you constantly attend to outrage, the world will begin looking hostile.

One of the most useful Stoic skills is creating distance between an impression and your response. Something happens, your mind produces an interpretation, your body reacts, and instead of immediately turning all of that into behavior, you wait.

Stoicism becomes especially useful here because it asks you to separate responsibility from control. You are responsible for your preparation, conduct, judgment, effort, and response. You are not responsible for forcing reality to reward those things exactly as you hoped.
A person who cannot tolerate discomfort becomes dependent on relief. And once relief becomes necessary, discipline becomes difficult.

There is always someone telling you what should matter, what success should look like, what you should buy, fear, admire, pursue, reject, or become. The pressure does not always feel like pressure because it arrives through repetition.
You do not need to wake up inspired every morning. You need a mind that can still choose well when inspiration does not arrive.

t: Self-Authority
q: Self-authority might be mistaken for confidence, because confident people often seem to have it. But it is something quite different. Confidence is being sure of a decision. Self-authority is being sure of who gets to make it.

Watch a controlling boss and a people-pleasing employee in the same meeting. They look like opposites, one seizing opportunities, one disappearing into the views of others, but they are both reacting.
Deference and control in the face of others' authority are not opposites. They are two extremes that arise when self-authority has not been established.
Self-authority recognizes the authority of others as much as the authority of self. It has to, that's what makes it a boundary and not just a claim.

On one reading, self-authority is the moral-psychological cousin of what Robert Kegan calls self-authoring in his stages of adult development, the capacity not just to hold values, but to step outside the systems and relationships that were handed you as your values, and choose among them for yourself.
So the question isn't whether you're certain. It's whether you're willing, to claim what's yours, to leave what isn't, and to bear all that entails.

t: Manufactured Urgency Is Not the Same as Discipline
q: Manufactured urgency can lead to burnout, mainly because you set a deliberately made-up deadline that has no natural ending. If you don't have an alarm to tell you when to stop, then damage is around the corner.
The problem with manufactured urgency as it is usually practiced is that we disguise controlled motivation (do it or else) as autonomous motivation (I don't want to do it, but I want the outcome).
I needed to perform because I wanted to keep being the smart kid, as if my identity were merely tied to results.

Not only that, but for animals, stress stops after the threat has gone away. We have gotten used to keeping our alarm on. The stress, the threat, never really leaves our heads. This eventually builds up and can become chronic if untreated.
Prioritizing and leaving space between finishing one milestone and starting something new gives your brain the rest it needs to avoid burnout.

Once you assess the situation and decide, you can enforce the deadlines. For this, motivation is key: focus on how what you need to do aligns with what you want to do, rather than on what you would lose if you don't do it.

t: Lessons from the First Statewide Mandate on School Start Times
q: We find that SB 328 increased the share of students sleeping at least 8 hours per night by 13%, meeting the CDC-recommended minimum for this age group.

Average mental health effects are imprecisely estimated, but boys show significant reductions in sadness, hopelessness, and suicidal ideation, and Hispanic students, who experienced the largest sleep-timing shifts, show parallel reductions in difficulty concentrating.
Math and English scores in grade 8 improved by approximately 0.08-0.10 standard deviations, with the largest gains among Hispanic and economically disadvantaged students.

A within-state analysis using teachers' commute arrival times as a proxy for pre-policy school start times corroborates these findings, and shows academic gains accumulating over 2023-2025 alongside a suggestive decline in high school dropout rates.

There seemed to be broad agreement that later school start times would be better, for all the reasons you might expect: better sleep leads to better mental health and better academic outcomes. But the community wasn't unanimously behind any of the proposed alternatives, there was no solution that was cost-free, and so the School Board eventually dropped the issue.

It is true that there are costs involved with changing school start times, including adapting bus routes and sports schedules and disrupting family routines. But this study provides new evidence that the gains for students are real, and the juice may be worth the squeeze.

t: IDIONOMO: The Intersection of the Idiographic and the Nomothetic
q: The science of reading and culturally responsive, asset-based practice are not merely compatible but mutually dependent, one without the other is incomplete. These frameworks are not in opposition, effective instruction for English learners requires both.
Systematic and explicit language instruction cannot replace cultural and linguistic responsiveness; it has to exist underneath it.

The assignment asks preservice teachers to conduct an ethnographic observation of one multilingual or multidialectal child over two to three weeks, across classroom, cafeteria, playground, and hallway, and to interview the classroom teacher, ESOL teacher, and family when possible.
The MLA is not designed for an entire class, it is designed to change how a teacher sees one child, so that they see all children differently afterward.

According to the Georgia Department of Education, universal screener data from the first year of the state's literacy coaching initiative showed a 15% improvement in student reading outcomes in participating high-need elementary schools, with the strongest gains reported in kindergarten (GaDOE, 2025).
Language knows no limits but the spirit of a second-language learner can languish when it bumps up against limitations imposed by the instructional constraints of the classroom.

t: How to Turn Information Into Knowledge You Can Remember and Use
q: You read a chapter, highlight a brilliant quote, and think, Wow, that makes total sense. I know this now. Researchers call this the illusion of fluency. Having a saved highlight or ChatGPT nearby doesn't mean the knowledge is available within your own thinking.
A smooth study session is often a poor learning session. Rereading and highlighting feel productive, but they only build familiarity, not recall.
The transfer of knowledge is notoriously difficult because novices get distracted by the surface features of a problem, while experts see the underlying structure.
Often, early competence and visible progress are what create motivation, not the other way around.
I spent years waiting for books to magically make me smarter. It didn't start working until I stopped treating learning as something that automatically happens when information passes in front of me.

t: How to Stop Presenting in the Middle of Your Own Workshop
q: It catches experienced facilitators because it feels productive from the inside. You're explaining something, the room is nodding, and every signal you get says this is going well.

Five minutes is the ceiling. If you've been speaking for five minutes and the group hasn't done anything, you're presenting, whatever you planned to be. The trouble is you won't notice five minutes passing. It feels like two.
Notes are a transcript of what you said. Outputs are evidence of what they concluded. Only one of those changes anything on Monday.
If you're on your feet at the front and everyone is seated facing you, the room has become a stage and audience. Physical setup tells the group who is meant to perform and who is meant to receive.

There's a fast test for any slide. Does it hold an answer or a question? Answers are presentation slides. Questions are facilitation slides. Most decks run about eighty per cent answers, which means most of the slides are doing the thinking the participants should be doing.
The reversal is always physical first, because you can't talk a room out of passivity. You can only hand them something to do that makes being passive impossible.

t: How to Avoid Tragedy: Study Tragedy
q: How many pieces of literature have shown us the dangers of masking one's identity, overvaluing ambition and status, using words and power to manipulate others, and collapsing under the weight of revealed reality?

Oedipus is a man of high status who has a complicated background. He is held in high regard for his intelligence, adored across the land. And he claims to bring peace and opportunity to a downtrodden people.
Oedipus, after fighting against a plague, comes to realize he is the plague. He has brought about his own downfall.
The blindness, the obsession with status, the unrelenting adherence to a fated fall, they stuck to their stories, when letting go might have saved them.

But many of the famous tragic works of literature from our culture had a character offering a way out, or at least a way through. There are teachers and advisors offering wisdom, clowns and choruses acting as consciences, hinting at ways the stars of our stories might take a closer look at themselves.
As I wrote in a long essay a few weeks ago, the purpose of education is to help us survive. The humanities, specifically, do that by teaching us to remember the lessons of the past.

t: How Do You Spend Your Status?
q: Leaders who focus only on the personal benefits of status miss a tremendous opportunity to motivate and inspire people. In contrast, the best leaders can't wait to spend their status on others.

Good leaders view their status and influence as a currency meant to circulate, not a privilege to hoard. They spend it deliberately on those around them who need a lift-up, an opportunity to showcase their skills, or a moment to feel special.
The question isn't whether a leader has status. Almost every leader does, in some measure. The question is what they spend it on.
Leaders who want to spend their status well start small. They look for one person each week who could use an advocate, an introduction, or a word of credit in front of others.
Status spent on others doesn't disappear. It compounds. The leader who gives status away generously always ends up with more of it.
The leaders we remember the most aren't the ones who climbed the highest, but the ones who reached back to lift others.

t: Historical Truth Is an Odyssey
q: Odysseus is not merely the founding hero of Western literature. He is its founding unreliable narrator. And the particular form of his unreliability turns out to illuminate, with uncomfortable precision, two centuries of the most consequential cultural argument in the modern world.

Homer signals as much at the very outset: the hero's crew was destroyed, he tells us, because they heedlessly devoured the sun-god's cattle. But that is strikingly different from what Odysseus says happened. The two accounts contradict each other, and Homer's comes first.

Juvenal, writing in the early second century AD, identified the mechanism precisely: Odysseus stirred his listeners to anger and laughter alike as a mendax aretalogus, a lying virtue-signaller, to use a translation our own age might find disconcertingly contemporary, before naming the decisive reason he could get away with it.
The Ithacan's tale was all his own, with none to bear him witness. No surviving companions, no contradicting testimony, no check on the account except the credulity of his hosts.

Lord Byron, poet, philhellene, and the most eloquent prosecutor of Lord Elgin ever to take the stand, is routinely invoked as a kind of disinterested moral witness: the conscience of the age, catching a Scottish earl red-handed on the Acropolis.

Classical Wisdom has previously published arguments in favor of their return. But an intellectual conversation is richer when we are willing to seriously consider arguments with which we may disagree.

t: Give Me 20 Minutes and I'll Make You Impossible to Manipulate
q: People at this stage of cognition treat authority as ground truth. They obey their priest, parents, teachers, textbook, or favorite influencer or celebrity rather than evaluating ideas based on merit and critical thought.
Social media algorithms don't show you what you want, they show you what you're most likely to react to - trapping you in a lower level of thinking.

Short-form attention hacking content has no through-line. No greater purpose. No sense making. Thousands of meaningless ideas flood our mind and we are unable to make sense of the chaos, trapping us in a low-consciousness state.
Stupidity begins when you find an answer that feels to good to keep testing or exploring. The answer hardens into identity, and from then on any challenge feels like an attack.

The uncurated feed is junk food for the mind. If you default to the main feed, you're eating whatever gets served at the world's largest buffet, and the food is engineered for addiction and cheap dopamine.
The NCP doesn't stop being an NPC because he reads Nietzsche. He becomes an NPC who quotes Nietzsche.
The world doesn't need more consumers. It needs more of what only you can create.

t: Getting Students to Share Their Half-Formed Gray Mist
q: I think people often misconceive of tutoring as explaining. Sometimes that's true, hey today we're going to learn about photosynthesis, but a lot of times you're trying to get the kid to blurt out the half-formed gray-mist idea in their head so that you can help clarify. They're sort of stuck and you get them unstuck.
AI is a very good explainer, but the behavior we see in randomized trials so far is the kid simply will not reveal their misunderstanding to the AI.

Silva knows the student speaks Spanish and also notices the student using her arms to describe skew lines, lines that meet. Silva wants to draw out the student's half-formed gray-mist ideas about parallel lines so she uses the languages the student seems to speak comfortably, both Spanish and embodied, to clarify parallel lines.

If you're a school leader, I think you can ask yourself a couple of interesting questions here. You can ask yourself, at what point in the future will chatbot tutors offer my students even 5% of what Silva has offered her students?

The entrenched hostility in tech land to teachers is so strange and deep, is it just because it's a care profession? Because it has soft skills they don't like? Why is that the job that they're so keen to put on the chopping block?
We're seeing more and more schools succeed by leveraging technology thoughtfully. But that success is never about the technology alone. The teachers and administrators deserve most of the credit.

t: Can You Just Shut Up?
q: Before they finish their sentence, we're ready with our response. Ready to show how smart we are, how much we know, or how quickly we can solve the problem.

Marcus Aurelius reminded himself to do just that, saying that he needed to get into the habit of listening attentively to anything that anyone says, and enter, as much as you can, into the mind of the speaker.
To enter into another person's mind, even for a moment, we first need to get out of our own head. We have to stop rehearsing our answer. Stop preparing the clever thing we're going to say next.

When I'm waiting for the person I'm interviewing to break a silence by giving me a piece of information I want, I write SU (for Shut Up!) in my notebook. If anyone were ever to look through my notebooks, he would find a lot of SUs there.
Silence is the weapon, Caro said, silence and people's need to fill it, as long as the person isn't you.

t: America's Demoralized Men, Part II: Lost Pathways, Greater Struggles https://ifstudies.org/report-brief/americas-demoralized-men-part-ii-lost-pathways-greater-struggles
a: Joseph E. Davis, Michael Toscano, and Ken Burchfiel
q: Demoralized is the term we use to characterize a state of mind reflected in agreement with such self-appraisals as I am inclined to think that I am a failure (43%), and such expressions of powerlessness as I often feel that I have little control over the things that happen to me (61%), and of being found insufficient, such as I never seem to do enough to please people (54%).

In fact, 4 out of 10 young men have two or fewer close friends, which includes 1 in 3 (34%) with one to two close friends and almost 1 in 10 (9%) who report zero close friends. The best predictor of having three or more friends is connection to institutions like marriage, church, and school.
Nearly three-quarters of young men either strongly (27%) or somewhat strongly (45%) endorse this anti-meritocratic belief; just 7% strongly disagree.

But that is not what we found, not even close. Even to the greater-opportunities statement, 75% think it describes them at least somewhat well. Similarly, 81% and 84% of respondents say the same about their capacities and ambition, respectively.

Of those who watch pornography many times a day or more, 43% experience loneliness, 36% feel depressed, and 29% are anxious. Feeling like a failure is also closely tied to these activities. For example, 66% of daily gamblers and 63% of daily pornography watchers, compared to 42% of men as a whole, report feeling like a failure.

The loss of institutionalized pathways and defined roles, and the simultaneous shift of responsibility to individuals to create their own career and life trajectories have introduced a great deal of precariousness into the lives of young men and left them bereft of guidance and structure.

Married men with kids are around half as likely (16%) to have current anxiety, bipolar disorder, or depression as those who are married without kids (31%) and those who are unmarried without kids (31%).

t: You're Not Delegating. You're Assigning.
q: For years I redid my team's work. Not all of it. But enough that I'd get something from them, look at it, and think it's faster if I just fix this myself.
Looking back, what I was actually doing was making sure nobody ever got better at it. Nobody learns from work that gets fixed without them ever hearing about it.

There's a big difference between giving someone responsibility and giving someone ownership. Responsibility means they have a task to do, the one written in their job description. Ownership means they're accountable for the result, and with that comes the authority to make decisions they also own.
I stopped asking what needs to get done this week and started asking what needs to get done without me. That sounds like a small shift. But small hinges swing big doors.
Most of the time the answer is no. Most of what was going through me didn't need me. It needed a clear standard, a defined outcome, somebody trained to it, and permission to decide.

They can tell when every real decision travels up. They don't usually say it, but the good ones start calculating whether this is a place they can grow into something bigger, or whether they've already hit the ceiling.

t: When The Weather Walks Into The Classroom
q: Research in environmental psychology shows that weather affects mood, attention, sensory processing, and even executive function, but in the staff rooms I've been in, teachers often discussed how their students' behaviour had changed before this research came to light.

Wind increases sensory input, and it activates the nervous system. It often puts students on standby for fallen objects or large things like branches and leaves that could be blown around in the wind. Sometimes the wind can trigger a fightIorIflight response.

Rain reduces natural light, which affects alertness and mood, and it can lower serotonin levels. It also keeps students indoors during breaks, which means less movement, less fresh air, and more pentIup energy.

One 12-year-old student once said to me, "Miss, it feels like my brain's all foggy." And when I looked around the class, I could see that a lot of students' body language indicated that it probably felt the same way for them too.
Sunlight boosts dopamine and serotonin, which is great for making students feel good about the day, but it's often not so wonderful for focus.
I swapped it for a carousel of short, active tasks with clear, simple outcomes. I built in movement, and I added a calming starter.

I've found that students rarely have the metacognitive awareness to recognise how external factors shape their internal state. But once they do, they begin to understand that their struggles are responses to the environment they are in.

t: The Three Body Problem and Assessment Design
q: Every suite of course assessments often has to answer to several moving targets at once: an industry partner's sense of what counts as job-ready, an institution-wide capability framework, course learning outcomes, and, running underneath all of them, whatever the current generation of AI tools can already do.

Long Stable Eras alternate with Chaotic Eras that arrive without warning and can destroy a civilisation outright. The Trisolarans respond by dehydrating themselves, reducing their bodies to something inert and storable, and waiting out the chaos until a stable window opens again.

Whichever voice is loudest that semester wins, so the task ends up shaped by pressure rather than by design, and the coordinator spends the semester firefighting instead of coordinating. Because nothing was ever declared non-negotiable, validity erodes, until someone asks what the task is actually evidence of.
This is the restricted three-body problem, and it produces Lagrange points: positions where a body too small to influence the two giants can still hold a relatively stable relationship with them.

CLOs earn that priority by choice, not by nature. The coordinator declares them the first claim on the design for the teaching period. This is where agency enters: the giants outside a course aren't yours to move, but what gets priority inside it is.

There will be no closed-form solution that makes assessment design stable once and for all. Fixing the CLOs as the central mass gives you a system that can be continuously rebuilt (subject to resourcing!) without losing its educational purpose.

t: The Spotify Student: Reckoning with Audiobooks
q: Both the 2024 National Assessment of Educational Progress report (commonly referred to as the Nation's Report Card) and the Manhattan Institute's thorough analysis of that report indicate that the decline in literacy predates the pandemic.

The audiobook reader has already made the critically important interpretive decisions for the listener, thus preempting the most important objective of any humanities course: that is, to train students in careful, close, interpretative reading skills. The students do not actually have to read at all when using audiobooks.

High school teachers on the ground confess that the majority of their students are employing audiobooks. As a result, the students have difficulty locating key passages in the text; understanding important developments in plot, character, and the use of words; and recognizing the beauty and elegance of the writing.

Puzzling over a passage, worrying over it, teasing out its implications, relishing its beauty, craft, and humor—these are the activities of a thoughtful, active mind at work when reading an important piece of literature. Reading is discovering a word that delights the mind or a logical move that brings pleasure and new understanding.
Reading is about more than seeing words on the page or even reading those words. It is the student's interpretation and discovery of meaning that makes that student a reader.
When I first began teaching, our students made a firm commitment not to consult commentaries of any kind when studying great works of literature. It was even a written policy in our student handbook.

t: The Question You Skip Is the One That Decides It
q: Nine research assistants read through a sample of 368 transcripts and hand-labeled the question types. They found six: introductory, mirror, full-switch, partial-switch, follow-up, and rhetorical. Follow-ups made up 44% of all questions asked, more than any other type.

Brooks describes follow-up questions as the superheroes of conversation. They are the opposite of topic-switching questions, since they hold you on the present subject and probe deeper into something the other person already said.
Researchers found that a participant who asked just one more question on each of their 20 dates would get one additional yes across those dates, on average. One question. One extra outcome.

Brooks also names two question types that do nothing for you. Introductory questions open a conversation and are necessary. Mirror questions reciprocate what was just asked, as in answering "how are you" and returning it, and her research found the likability boost applies to neither.

Apathy. A potential questioner, such as a manager, may simply not care about the answers, feeling disinterest in what the other person has to say. Her response to that is direct: the apathy is often misplaced, since we have much to learn from others and perhaps especially from people lower in status than ourselves.

Set an explicit number before you walk in. Her advice is to go into the conversation thinking you need to ask at least five questions, or that you need to ask questions, listen to the answers, and ask follow-ups.

t: The Back to School AI Stack, Rated
q: Free tiers in ed tech are the least stable thing in your entire toolkit. They get generous when a company is chasing teachers, and they get tight when the company starts chasing districts. Both of those things happened this summer.

Paste an article, a URL, a PDF, or just a topic, and Diffit hands back the same content at multiple reading levels with comprehension questions and vocabulary pulled from the passage itself. Second grade through high school, plus translation into a long list of languages.

The free tier caps how much you can generate, and it does not save your output history. That second one bites harder than it sounds: generate something great in September, want it again in January, and it is gone.

In mid-July, the free plan changed. Individual free accounts now get five Space launches per year. Not per month. Per year. Your onboarding Space does not count against it, and referrals earn two more sessions each, but the practical ceiling is roughly one Space per grading period.
Diffit charges you in exports. The work is unlimited, but getting it into Google Docs is not. MagicSchool charges you in memory. Generate freely, but do not expect to find it again.
Anyone who built a routine on the old always-free tier is going to hit a wall this fall and be surprised by it.

t: Strat Chat - 'We Do' Checks for Understanding
q: An example problem pair is something I only began to utilize this year after having a discussion with a math teaching colleague and realizing that it was a tool they used constantly which I was not realizing had so much potential in the Humanities subjects I teach.

The example problem pair pairs the power of the worked example effect with the feeling of independent success which comes from a You Do. Almost a You Do with training wheels on as the teacher thinks aloud and solves a question step by step on one side of the board before asking students to complete a similar, yet slightly different problem on the other side with their example remaining on the board as a scaffold to work from.

A check for understanding is all about feedback, both for the teacher and the student. But feedback without action is just noise. Unless we do something with the feedback, then it's just empty words to the benefit of nobody.

First you need to conduct any other check for understanding where students either write, say or do something. Then the teacher provides feedback (hopefully constructive) before asking the students to write, say or do their response again, but better!
The example problems need to be alike in how the knowledge is applied otherwise the worked example could potentially mislead students or even add further to their cognitive load.
Too much scaffolding and students haven't had to think hard enough to move to independence. Too much independence and students will not have had the practice they need to know where to start.

t: Schools, Civilization, and The Odyssey
q: Telemachus is following the rules of xenia, an ancient Greek concept of hospitality or, as it is sometimes translated, "guest-friendship". There are rules about what should be offered (food and wine) and when business should be discussed (after the food and wine) and who should receive the hospitality (strangers, foreigners, the poor, and anyone else who properly asks for it).

Homer repeatedly contrasts characters who do their duty with those who don't. The consequences do not always fall to the shirkers themselves, but they are often felt by the people around them as tragedy swallows their friends and family.

It is the basis of civilized life, actually, to treat strangers with kindness and follow rules that may inconvenience the individual for the betterment of all. It is no accident, after all, that polite rule-followers may be described as civil, and a collection of polite rule-followers may be called a civilization.
Teachers are the opposite of the "disorganized raiders" Yglesias criticizes for their role in societal decline. Teachers are caretakers at home, keeping the kingdom while everyone else is out to sea.

A family can show up at the schoolhouse door on Monday, and by Tuesday the bus will come to their house to pick up their child. The yellow school bus is not quite a limousine, but it's not far off from that level of service.
When teachers care for other people's children, they set in motion an inter-generational social contract and remind us that we are more prosperous when we look out for each other.

t: Pay Attention, Be Astonished
q: Every tradition that has taken attention seriously has answered that question the same way: not by leaving it undirected, but by choosing, deliberately, what it should be for.
But focusing on one's breath is only the proximate object. Regardless of what you're assigned, Buddhism has a universal, non-negotiable aim: liberation from suffering.

The investor Charlie Munger had a line for this: "Show me the incentive and I'll show you the outcome." Tristan Harris has spent years tracking what that principle produces in social media platforms built to hold your attention.

Their word for the danger of an untethered mind was acedia — a kind of spiritual paralysis that could leave a monk unable to summon the will to pray, work, or do much of anything else. A wandering mind was more than a lapse in productivity; it was threatening to the whole purpose of a monk's life.

Silicon Valley optimizes for an incentive it inherited, not one it chose. Profit-from-attention came from the market; their engineers are tasked with chasing it. The monks chose their object first, then built around it.

When the aim goes unnamed, our students default to the system's incentives. Their aim becomes compliance — achievement, competition, a grade. An aim revealed by default requires no reflection, no consideration, and no critical thought.

t: Just Show Me the Prompt
q: AI has made it effortless to generate text. Beautiful, structured, confident-sounding text. And people are using that power generously. Too generously. Documents that could fit on one page now arrive as fifteen.
I now use AI to summarize the documents that others used AI to write. We have built a closed loop: a document laundering machine where AI inflates on one end and AI compresses on the other.
A long AI-generated document can hide the fact that the author never thought deeply about the problem at all. Length becomes a disguise, and a very convincing one.
If you used AI to write a document, your prompt is the truest artifact of your thinking. A sharp, specific prompt shows that you understood the problem. A vague prompt shows that you did not.
Asking for the prompt cuts straight to what matters, faster than reading twenty pages ever could. It is not rude. It is the most respectful thing you can do with someone's time.
Set expectations early. One page is almost always enough. Two pages should be a conscious choice. If someone sends you twenty pages, ask for a one-page summary before you invest your time.

t: How Ofqual are Killing English
q: Gove told us he had had enough of experts, and called teachers, academics and their unions who opposed him "the Blob". He pushed forward the Labour intitiative of academisation which may or may not have improved schools.
Between 2000 and 2009, England dropped down the rankings table from 7th to 25th for reading, 8th to 27th in maths, and 4th to 16th in science.

It was a simple and brilliant idea - The National Reference Test. A sample of each year 11 would sit a one hour paper in each of maths and English. The results would be kept from students and schools, so they would never be misused as accountability measures.

For the past couple of years, the test has detected that attainment around the 4/5 borderline in English language is weaker than when the test was first administered in 2017. If the process worked as intended, this would have led Ofqual to require grade boundaries to be changed so that fewer pupils achieved a grade 9-4 in English language.

Over that same period, teachers have become more focused on evidence, on research, on retrieval - their teaching has clearly improved. This is also borne out by the rise in the number of schools Ofsted has declared not to be failing.

To our shame, English teams overwhelmingly practise these ridiculous forms of writing - description overloaded with adverbs and adjectives, spurious colours, redundant vocabulary, arbitrary single word sentences and single sentence paragraphs.
Writing has become a ludicrous ticklist of turgid tricks to cross off in the exam paper, and in the curriculum.

t: Classroom Management is All About One Thing
q: Classroom management is all about creating an environment in which student behaviors are conducive to enjoyable and productive learning experiences. "Enjoyable and productive": that's the key framing language to use with students and with ourselves.
We have our rules and procedures and management moves not because we like controlling young people, but rather because we are so darn in love with enjoyable and productive learning experiences.
Okay, now keep your hand up if you've ever found that to be annoying or frustrating." Most hands stay up.

Not because I'm a control freak, not because I don't want to hear everything you have to say, but because in a room full of thirty-two students there's got to be a way to protect an enjoyable and productive experience.
Though there's plenty more to classroom management, the master move is to frame it in a way that's clear and desirable for all parties.
Being annoyed or frustrated because of undisciplined speaking? Not enjoyable, not productive.

t: Catch Me If You Can
q: Last week I ran one of my own posts through Substack's new AI scanner. I wrote roughly 95% of it with a few assisted polishings here and there. The Substack AI Detector flagged it anyway. So I tried the reverse. I gave an AI a single prompt, took what it handed back, barely touched it, and scanned that. 30% human.

The most comprehensive independent test of AI-text detectors, published in the International Journal for Educational Integrity, found that none of the fourteen tools evaluated reached 80 percent accuracy, and performance fell apart further once text was edited or paraphrased.

A Stanford study in Patterns found detectors misclassified essays by non-native English writers as AI-generated at an average false positive rate of 61 percent, while handling native-speaker essays nearly perfectly. What these tools actually flag is a style, and they punish writers whose style doesn't fit the pattern.
That same Stanford team found that a single follow-up prompt asking the model to elevate its language dropped detection rates from 100 percent to 13. Students will learn that trick in a week.

A randomized controlled trial at Harvard found students learned more than twice as much in less time with an AI tutor, but that tutor was built deliberately around pedagogical best practice, giving one step at a time and refusing to hand over full solutions. The design did the work, not the model.
So the assignment can't be "don't use AI," and it can't be "we'll catch you if you do." The assignment is: bring me your prompt history. Show me what the first draft gave you and what you rejected.

t: Carrying On the Good Work of Others
q: He decided to run across Canada on an artificial leg to raise money for cancer research. He called it the Marathon of Hope.
Terry understood that the Marathon of Hope couldn't depend on just himself. He wanted Canadians to continue it without him.
He helped launch the Terry Fox Run in 1981 at more than 760 locations in Canada and around the world. In that first year, more than 300,000 people participated and raised more than $3.5 million.

His real achievement wasn't completing the run but in convincing millions of people that they could pick up something unfinished and carry it forward. Thanks to the leadership of Isadore Sharp, that's exactly what happened.
Leaders often think their job is to finish what they start. Terry Fox's legacy suggests something equally valuable: building on the important work of others.

If leadership is about making people and situations better, then expanding the influence of a great idea is what good leaders do. Terry Fox proved that a project embraced and taken up by a vast community becomes nearly unstoppable.

t: Careers Education
q: When a young person does not even know that a particular kind of job exists, it is impossible for them to express interest in it.

I began to reflect on the Response to Intervention model (also known as Multi-Tiered Systems of Support) we use at my school for guiding interventions in literacy, numeracy, behaviour and other areas. This begins with good Tier 1 instruction for all students.

All students are taught a deliberately planned and sequenced curriculum that gives the basics of a wide range of careers in different sectors, with a deliberate skew towards rewarding careers that students may have had little personal contact with.

Firstly, the curriculum is now dependent on the personal connections of people who work at the school or for the careers advice service. So, students will not necessarily be exposed to the widest range of relevant careers.

Education is not simply preparation for work. It is a deeper process of developing knowledge of the world that may well make young people more employable, but that will also give them a fulfilling life and a cultural hinterland.
I knew about jobs I had seen. I knew about teaching and being a doctor. I knew about engineering because my dad was an engineer.

t: Atomisation in Literacy
q: Atomisation is a reasonably intuitive idea in math class. Break a math skill into small chunks, teach one chunk at a time, and build bit by bit toward larger ideas.
The key insight of atomisation is that it's hard to learn two things at the same time. If students don't know what "first person" means, that definition up there won't make much sense.
Next up, I want students to retrieve that atom. This is where that learning moves securely into long-term memory.

The most important step of this whole thing is expansion. Expansion means I want to expand the contexts in which students are using this knowledge. One risk of atomisation is that breaking learning down into small steps means those steps become isolated.

Atomise, retrieve, expand," is my reminder: atomisation is useful, but only if students retain the atom and apply it in lots of different ways. Atomisation alone risks turning the curriculum into a bunch of isolated, disconnected bits of knowledge.

It's tempting to believe that, if only we could identify all the little atoms and relationships between them, we could build a machine to teach all those little atoms in the right order and make sure every student learns. That's the dream of lots of education technology right now.

t: A Catholic Educator's Evaluation
q: The Front Royal Statement is for Catholic education what the Declaration of Independence was to the American revolutionary colonists: an outline of the basic principles and grievances on which their new nation was born.
The seven principles establish a rich vision of education that classical educators resonate with. And they do so without using the language of "classical.

One of the loveliest lines in the Front Royal Statement reiterates that education is a "restauratio" that heals "the wounds of sin to reorder the soul in an ascent from dispersion to unity. t: Why Coaching Taught Me to Stop Solving

Portraying curriculum content, presenting ideas accurately without oversimplifying them into meaninglessness. Enlisting student participation, getting kids to engage without losing the thread of the lesson. Containing student behavior, keeping order without shutting down the very risk-taking that learning requires.

The trick, and the part that took me a while to internalize, is that these problems compete with each other. Push harder on participation and you may lose your grip on behavior. There's no clean sequence where you check off 'curriculum' and move to 'participation.'
Kennedy tells me which problem is showing up. Lefstein gives me a lens to look inside that problem when it's happening through talk, which, in an English classroom, is most of the time.

t: Separating a Decision From the Emotion Connected to It
q: Research consistently confirms that the strong emotions tied to a decision can change what leaders pay attention to, how they interpret information, and how they weigh risks and rewards.

For instance, when a potential choice feels good, people tend to perceive it as less risky and more beneficial. The opposite is also true. When a prospective decision feels bad, people see greater risk and more downside, even when the objective evidence doesn't justify that evaluation.

Rather than mentally rehearsing a choice as 'I need to figure out if I should do this,' more effective leaders learn to silently reframe the decision in the third person or by role: 'Should the CEO take this deal?' 'Is this the right call for us?'

So, instead of asking how they feel about the decision right now, better leaders consider how they will feel about the choice in six weeks or six months. This forces a shift from an immersed, present state to a more distanced, evaluative one.
Ultimately, great decision-making isn't about eliminating emotion but about creating enough distance to see clearly through it.

t: How to Speed Up Your Onboarding as an Engineering Leader

For every dimension I care about, I ask three specific questions: The negative limit, the worst thing the company has accepted or done in this area. The middle point, the most common approach. The positive limit, the best thing that ever happened.

q: The challenge with difficult decisions isn't usually uncertainty about the missing piece of information. The problem is anxiety, the emotional discomfort of not really knowing what the narrative actually is, caught between two or more frames that conflict in your head.

Dismissal: The largest group (!) ~33% of all responses. These commentators barely engaged with the author's framing at all, didn't acknowledge the hesitation, and offered flat judgement instead. 'Nobody cares. You are overthinking it,' was their verdict.
Going back to the thread, what's also worth noticing is that the author didn't bring just one frame. They brought two, and that's what triggers the emotional response, the anxiety and confusion.

t: Great Business Leaders Love the Flywheel
q: A business is not a group of departments; it is a network of interdependencies. Sales promises what product has yet to deliver. The product roadmap gets impacted by what support hears during the last escalation.

A flywheel is heavy and slow at the start. Every push seems to accomplish nothing. Then the pushes begin to compound, and eventually momentum starts to build. The catch is that the pushes have to land in the same place.

Amazon's loop started with book selection and a great customer experience. A better experience brought more traffic. Traffic attracted third-party sellers. More sellers meant more selection, which improved the experience again.
No single move on that list is clever. A competitor could have copied any one of them. What was hard to copy was the loop because it only pays out when all parts of it are running.

In almost every business, one component is quietly throttling the rest, and it is rarely the one getting the most attention. Fix that part, and everything you have already built starts working harder.

t: The Cowardice of False Modesty

Humility is understanding that everything you have comes from God and belongs to God. Magnanimity is understanding that it's because of that that you are responsible for doing something good with it.
According to Aquinas, the pusillanimous man sins not because he has wrongly estimated his gifts but because he has refused to even look for and use them.
