t: Memory Is the Residue of Thought: The Seven Blind Mice Lesson
q: Daniel Willingham's simple observation that "memory is the residue of thought." We have all heard or seen the quote before.

Before I ever select a strategy, prompt, technique, response structure, or question, I need to know exactly what I want students to remember. Otherwise, it is very easy to create a lesson where students are simply busy working, writing diligently, and completing assignments all without necessarily devoting much of their working memory to the information they actually need to remember.

Each technique served the same underlying purpose: I was continually directing students' attention and thinking back toward the specific information I wanted them to remember. The students weren't going to just hear the order and colors of the mice as I read the story.
When students understand that retrieval practice strengthens their ability to bring knowledge back to mind, that changes how they view retrieval tasks I assign.

That principle became concrete for my students during the first day of school this year. I wanted to give students an immediate, memorable example of what I would soon be teaching them about learning, working memory, attention, remembering, forgetting, and the importance of thinking to memory.
Their strong memories provided the evidence I needed. They had thought about those details repeatedly, and when I asked them to retrieve those details the next day, they were able to do it.

t: How a Focus on Results and Compassion Reinforce Each Other

Chambers' leadership style reveals a truth that many leaders miss. Performance and compassion are not competing priorities to be balanced against each other. They are mutually reinforcing actions.
Chambers built Cisco into one of the most successful companies of his era not despite his intensity, but because his intensity was matched by his humanity.

q: Knee-jerk reactions tend to have consequences. The problem in front of you is not necessarily THE problem.

t: Being Tired Changes What You See

t: A Care-Giver's Trials
q: Annie Morgan wrapped her arms around her eldest daughter's waist and guided her toward the minivan, the two of them moving in a slow, sideways shuffle.
At 13, Ava was nearly as big as Annie, who stands just five feet flat, 110 pounds.
Then something shifted. As Annie helped Ava into the vehicle, Ava wailed and slammed her body against the seat. The car rocked.
The struggle lasted six minutes: long enough for Annie to tighten one belt, then another. Long enough to block a blow to the head, catch Ava's hands and dodge them when she couldn't.

In one form or another, scenes like this unfold every morning in millions of American homes. Sons and daughters lifting aging parents out of bed. Spouses managing medications. Parents helping adult children get dressed.

t: What We Talk About When We Talk About the Love of Reading (Part II)
q: I pointed out that this decline is not just a recent trend, but one that stretches back more than 80 years. I also noted that not only are Americans reading less, but the same is true in the United Kingdom and Australia.

One widely noted study found that this only happened with the reading of literary fiction but not with popular fiction or non-fiction. Examining all the research on this issue suggests caution, and these same benefits have been accomplished by watching video narratives.

The claims about reading's purported positive impacts on critical thinking, memory, and cognition are supported only by correlational evidence. You can't tell if reading fosters those abilities or if those who are gifted in those areas are more likely to be readers.

The unsubstantiated idea that reading accords a sense of belonging seems to contradict actual data, teens who read more were less happy than those who read less, probably because of the isolation from social participation that it often requires.

t: The Art of Delegation
q: Delegation is commonly understood as the distribution of work. Its harder and more consequential form is handing over authority, and the two are not the same thing.

Authority is different because it transfers the right to be wrong. To delegate a decision is to accept that it may be made differently from how the leader would have made it, and occasionally made badly, without the matter returning for correction.
the authors found that more dominant chief executives maintained a significantly wider personal span of control and delegated fewer decision rights than their less dominant counterparts.
A talented person given a title but not the authority that should accompany it learns quickly that their judgment is not trusted, and that the interesting decisions will always be made elsewhere.

Delegation fails when leaders reclaim authority at the first sign of discomfort. The instinct to intervene is strongest precisely when intervention is most damaging, because a reasonable decision taken independently is often worth more to an organisation than a marginally better one that reinforces its dependence on a single person.

The organisations that outgrow their founders are not those whose leaders learned to distribute tasks more efficiently. They are those whose leaders learned to distribute the right to decide, and then, at the first uncomfortable test of that decision, declined to take it back.

t: The Anthropology of School Rituals
q: Rituals don't endure because they're the most efficient way of doing something but because they address deeper social issues that become part of the background of everyday life.

Through repeated acts of gathering, singing, speaking and remembering, societies continually renew what Durkheim called social solidarity: the shared sense that individuals belong to a moral community larger than themselves.

Psychologists Michael Norton and Francesca Gino have shown that rituals reduce anxiety and increase our sense of control even when there's no plausible way they could influence outcomes. Their power lies in changing our relationship to uncertainty.

t: Schemas and Curiosity
q: The SEEK model takes a slightly different approach, explaining how curiosity can change learning through the generation, maintenance, and restructuring of schemas. It incorporates the mechanisms outlined by Rumelhart and Norman in 1978: accretion, tuning, and restructuring.

The authors take the increasingly popular view that existing schemas generate predictions, emphasising the notion that schemas are active and dynamic, rather than things embedded within long-term memory. Furthermore, learning doesn't simply add to schemas, but also reorganises them as new information becomes available.

If, however, there is a significant discrepancy, a prediction error arises, triggering curiosity and metacognitive appraisal. This may involve the following evaluations: What is going on here? Is this discrepancy meaningful? Can I resolve it? Is finding out worth the effort?

For example, our animal schema might assume that all mammals give birth to live young. Enter the platypus. The schema readjusts from all mammals give birth to live young to most mammals give birth to live young, but some lay eggs.

Schema modification doesn't just mean the learner knows more; they now possess a different predictive model. The modified schema can lead to different and potentially more precise predictions. This means the learner becomes more sensitive to discrepancies, creating more prediction errors, which, in turn, fuels further curiosity.
On the darker side, how can the model explain how those with nefarious intent exploit the way the brain organises, updates, and re-writes the contents of these knowledge networks?

t: Having More Left Me With Less

It's time, they wrote in a recent post, for the field of social studies to have its "Sold a Story" moment - following the lead of the "science of reading" movement in rejecting ineffective practices in favor of those grounded in the science of learning.

t: Everyone Needs a Way to Externalize Their Thoughts
q: A thought that remains entirely inside your head can feel complete simply because it is familiar. You can circle around the same idea for hours and experience the movement as progress.
Journaling did not solve the transition. It did something more modest and, in the long run, more useful: it gave the experience a form I could examine.
The research on cognitive offloading shows that external tools can improve performance, especially when a task requires us to keep several pieces of information active at the same time.
There is a difference between storing a thought and developing one. A note that says "important" may preserve a reminder, but it does not necessarily help you understand the idea.
In their experiments, students who wrote by hand performed better on conceptual questions, and the researchers proposed that laptop note-taking encouraged more verbatim transcription.
The notebook is upstream. The AI system is downstream. That order protects the learner's agency.

t: Does Alpha School Work for Regular Kids?
q: Media coverage of Alpha School has generally focused on its claim that it educates children much faster than traditional models, specifically that it helps students "grow 2.6 times faster than peers on nationally normed MAP tests" and do it in two hours instead of six.
I'll meet the kid, and I'm like, listen, kiddo, this is up to you," says admissions director Cara Wilkinson. "This is not about your parents. This is about you.

Unbound Academy's enrollment application is, by law, much less selective than Alpha School's. A parent doesn't have to attest that their student is neurotypical, able-bodied, and well-behaved. They only have to meet the much lower bar of geographic residency.

Unbound Academy projected 60% proficiency in math off a baseline of 34% and ended the year with 10% compared to an Arizona state average of 34%. They projected 65% proficiency in ELA off a baseline of 40% and ended with 28% compared to an Arizona state average of 42%.

But Alpha School has not become nationally famous for its claims to grow student learning in some bounded capacity. It has become famous for the claims of its founder and principal that student learning is "limitless," and, indeed, that the Alpha School model will take students to the outer edges of academic achievement.
Their outcomes indicate that it is far harder to make successful students than it is to select them in advance.

t: Dearly Beloved, We Are Gathered Here Today to Get Through This Thing Called... Implementation.
q: The photocopier model of implementation: Senior leadership puts a beautifully crisp idea into the machine. By the time it has passed through six meetings, three PowerPoints and a departmental briefing, everyone is holding a slightly grey version with one corner missing.
Remarkably, use of mini-whiteboards increased by 600% during the 40 minutes in which senior leaders were walking around carrying clipboards.
We thought we had achieved alignment because everyone was using the same vocabulary. Unfortunately, they were using the same words to describe six different things.

One may think, "I need to demonstrate this technique during an observation." Another may think, "I need information about what pupils understand so I can decide what to do next." The second mental model is much more likely to produce intelligent adaptation than the first, which just becomes technique theatre.
The real test of whether something is embedded isn't whether people do it during a learning walk. It's whether they still do it in February, period 5, when the Wi-Fi has gone down.

Policies and checklists can create surface compliance, but they cannot specify the correct response to every situation. Instead, the more scalable approach is to develop shared, accurate mental models among the people making those decisions.

t: Build Something That Outlives You
q: Influence is something that's built over time, that's tied to real-world accomplishments, like building an institution, whether it's a church or a family. And consequently, influence is something that gathers slowly and has strong ties locally.

A person of influence, because their influence emanates from a local reality, is generally answerable to people who can actually confront them, which is quite different from an influencer whose accountability is derived from metrics such as audience capture and engagement.

Lawrence points out that with personal brands, the influencer becomes the marketing. This results in something that's called key man risk. The growth and morale of the congregation end up being substantially dependent on that one man's presence.

I remember a pastor on staff telling me that they had to conceal whether or not the senior pastor was preaching on a given Sunday because they would see a massive drop in attendance, something like 30%.

It's foolish to measure the health of your church by how influential your pastor is. Really, from an organizational standpoint, what you should be asking is: Is he increasingly making himself unnecessary?
The greatest measure of whether or not you built well is what happens after you are no longer there to hold it together.

t: Before August: A Year of Raising Both the Floor and the Ceiling
q: After a large gain from the 2023-24 year to the 2024-25 year, the third-grade ELA proficiency rate took a drastic drop from 54% in 2024-25 to 43% in 2025-26 - an 11-point decline in a single year.
This year, it jumped to 63%. That's a 12-point increase in a single year while the state fell 11 points - a 23-point swing overall.

In one year, the percentage of third graders performing at the highest tier increased from 18% to 47%. At the same time, our Level 1 percentage dropped from 13% down to 6%. We managed to move students at both ends of the spectrum.

MTSS is often talked about as a system for students who are behind. But that's only half of the job. The students who are already ahead need something from us, too. MTSS should raise the floor without lowering the ceiling.

Instead of worrying about teaching the program with rigid fidelity to the publisher's manual, we began using it as a flexible tool. We put a significant focus on both fluency building and vocabulary knowledge.
That's what a functioning MTSS system should look like: not a system that asks, "Who is below grade level?" but one that asks, "Where is every student right now, and what do they need next?

t: Against Toxic Femininity & Masculinity
q: But along the way, another idea emerged - fairness should mean equal division. Half the bills, half the cooking, half the cleaning, half the childcare, half the sacrifices. The appeal is easy to understand - a clear split seems to protect both people from being and feeling unfairly used.

Epictetus sometimes mocked people who expected circumstances to provide what simply wasn't available. He cautioned us against looking for figs in winter. Perfect 50/50 often belongs in the same category.
Domestic work has an odd feature - when it's done well, much of it disappears from view. The food is there. The electricity stays on. The passport hasn't expired. The child goes to see the dentist.
Mahler made it clear that there would be room for one composer in their household, and that composer would be him. Her life would have to accommodate the demands of his.
An unequal division of work can serve two people extremely well. But an unequal valuation of their lives is harder to survive.
I need you to handle bedtime three nights a week" gives another person something they can act on. "I can't keep carrying this level of financial responsibility" gives you a problem to solve together.
Because his life matters so much to her, preserving himself matters differently to him. She has made him, in his words, "more valuable to myself.

t: 1MW No. 318: Every Yes Has a Cost
q: By 2025, mobile orders were arriving faster than customers could get to the store. Baristas were trying to keep up with a stream of digital orders while also serving the customers standing directly in front of them.

There was nothing wrong with either idea. Convenience mattered, and connection mattered. The problem was trying to maximize both at the same time, through the same baristas, the same counters, and the same minutes.
Michael Porter calls this straddling: pursuing two different strategies without accepting the trade-offs required by either.
When people set their goals first, they tended to commit to more than their available time could realistically support. In effect, we give the same hour away more than once.
But when participants divided their available time before setting their goals, their goals became more realistic. They made more progress and were happier with the outcome.
Before saying yes to something new, ask: What will I have to say no to in order to say yes to this? If the answer is nothing, look again. Every yes costs something.

t: 1-to-1 Computer Initiatives: The Curious Case of Maine
q: 1-to-1 computer initiatives have one of the lowest effect sizes in the entire EdTech literature: approximately +0.12. That's less than one-third of the +0.42 benchmark commonly used to identify educational interventions with meaningful impact.

Between 1992 and 2002, Maine ranked among the nation's highest-performing education systems, with both fourth- and eighth-grade students consistently placing near the top of the country. Following the launch of MLTI, however, Maine's standing began a long-term decline.
By 2024, Maine had fallen from one of America's highest-performing education systems to roughly the middle of the pack in Grade 8, and the bottom quartile in Grade 4.
In 2017, 55% of Maine eighth-graders reported having access to a laptop in all classes, compared with just 15% in Massachusetts.

Unlike Maine, Massachusetts' national standing did not gradually erode over the next two decades: it strengthened. By 2002, Massachusetts had risen to the top of the nation in fourth-grade achievement - and by 2003, it had done the same in eighth grade.

Maine began this experiment as one of America's highest-performing education systems - but today, its eighth-graders sit roughly in the middle of the national pack, while its fourth-graders have fallen to the bottom quartile. After two decades, surely the burden of proof belongs with those still making the promises.

t: "Congrats! Now Go Talk to an Audience that Doesn't Want to Listen to You."
q: Every year we face SGO's, SGP's, walk-throughs, formal observations, action plans, and mountains of other paperwork, but students value our words much more than any of that stuff. I know this, because I experienced it when I was a student.
In high school, like many students, I lacked any sort of true self-confidence, I was constantly struggling to handle my emotions in a mature manner, and my social skills left a lot to be desired.

Mr. Romano had taught me three years earlier when I was a freshman, and I was sure he had forgotten me. In my mind, I was so insignificant that I was unworthy of note in his memory. But with a very brief interaction, Mr. Romano showed me I was wrong.
It's very possible Mr. Romano has completely forgotten our conversation, but I will remember it for the rest of my life.

Many educators in this room shared encouraging words with me when I was a struggling student teacher here ten years ago. Maybe you have forgotten about them, but I haven't. Your words make a difference. Always remember that.

This year you will be lucky enough to share in a student's joy, and a student will be lucky that they have someone like you to share in their sorrow. This year you will say something that a student will remember for the rest of their life.

t: Zuckerberg's Letter Shows Most Schools Are Getting AI Exactly Backwards
q: None of that lets educators off the hook. Because whatever you think of the messenger, the letter is a fairly accurate description of the world our students are walking into.
One student has a frontier model. The others don't. The letter tells you exactly who that student is.
Now look at the kid in your fourth-period class whose school blocked the model and whose family can't buy the subscription. Same age, same curiosity, no evening.
We did not eliminate the power asymmetry the letter warns about. We reproduced it inside the one institution built to interrupt it, and put an acceptable use policy on the door.
Restriction doesn't protect your students from wasting the tool. It protects them from having it.
The single largest expansion of access to individualized instruction in the history of formal education showed up, priced at zero or close to it, and the institutional response was to restrict it.
And the accreditors and standards bodies have been almost entirely silent. That's the load-bearing failure, because schools follow those signals.

t: Your TA Company Is Trapped in a Browser Tab. Time to Let Them Out (part 4 of 6)
q: That is not grading. That is data entry in a nicer outfit. Cowork ends that.
A full third of grading time is admin work around the actual grading. Opening tabs. Copying. Pasting. Formatting. Saving to the right folder. Uploading to the LMS.
Grant file access only to the folder you're about to use for grading. Not your whole drive. You don't need Cowork reading your taxes.
Those three items train the Desktop Assistant in your voice faster than any prompt. Samples beat descriptions every time.
Most teachers skip this and tell Cowork to grade everything in one go. Don't. The first feedback letter is your calibration shot.
If the feedback was too generic, add this line to RULES. If the same feedback could apply to two different students, it fails. Rewrite with specific quotes from the submission.

t: You Still Can't Fix Culture. Change What Keeps Producing It.
q: Its argument was simple. Culture emerged from how the organisation actually worked. Values workshops, leadership speeches and change programmes played supporting roles. Daily organisational life did the real work.
Culture is the patterned residue of people acting through roles within an organisational system. That gives culture its diagnostic value.
Successful organisation? Study the culture. Failing organisation? Change the culture. Merger struggling? Integrate the cultures. Strategy stalled? Build a performance culture.
When everything became cultural, culture lost its explanatory value. It became an organisational Rorschach test.
An executive may be asked to act for the enterprise while being rewarded for protecting a function. A manager may carry accountability for an outcome while authority remains several levels above.

A fragmented organisation can produce faster fragmentation. A confused organisation can automate confusion. A political organisation can encode yesterday's distribution of power into tomorrow's intelligent workflow.
Culture becomes useful when we treat it as evidence. A pattern has appeared. People are behaving in recognisable ways.

t: Why Teaching Maths Will Always Be Chalk and Talk (but the Chalk Might Sprout Wings)
q: There has always and will always be a part of teaching maths that is chalk and talk, standing at the front illustrating ideas with visual imagery and symbols. Arguably, this is because of a fundamental law of communicating maths, mathematics can only be conveyed in a combination of language, visual representation, symbolism and transformations over time.

So we use chalk (or its modern equivalent) because it allows us the dynamism to draw, notate and make changes all whilst talking them through it. It's quite a pantomime act, an art, a skill, all to be done within the tiny attention spans of reluctant children.

But good ones are hard to find, YouTube is designed to distract you with all manner of shiny lures, it's not trying to help you educate yourself. You have to wrestle the algorithm to give up the good stuff.
It uses Large Language Model process techniques to match White Rise Small steps the actual words spoken in the transcripts of the videos. So no miscuing by video title.

Chalk and talk will always be the main medium via which maths is passed forward, however, the chalk is now available in a variety of other formats, fancy graphics, animations, new forms of concrete, pictorial and symbolic (CPA), why shouldn't teaching be supplemented by making use of them?

t: What is Cognitive Load? Why Does it Matter?
q: The first is the complexity of the subject. A new prescription comes with complexity that's intrinsic to the task. You'll need to understand instructions, dosage, schedules, and refills.
Think of working memory as a truck that can carry a limited load. If the load is bigger than the capacity, things start to fall off. The same is true with the mind.

The problem is that chunking requires free working memory. If the mind is under pressure due to complexity, there aren't enough free resources for creating new chunks. So we read a dense scientific paper, but don't remember any of it.

In this example, the existing chunks of the nuclear physicist helped reduce the cognitive pressure and free up working memory. This is why what an audience already knows matters as much as what you're trying to teach them.
Intrinsic load: Complexity is all around us. This load represents how much processing is required to grasp the complexity of a subject, relative to the learner's existing knowledge.
The lesson: Manage the complexity of the subject you're communicating and make the presentation easier to consume.

t: What Sorority Rush and Male Influencer Culture Reveal About Young People Today
q: These look like unrelated phenomena. I don't think they are. Both are symptoms of the same underlying condition, a generation that has been handed extraordinary tools for self-presentation and almost no formation in how to become a self worth presenting.
Bama Rush is not really about sororities. It is about belonging, performed publicly, in an economy where belonging itself has become scarce and therefore valuable content.
Where Bama Rush sells belonging, the manosphere sells status and control, and it does so by first convincing young men that they have been cheated out of both.
A young man does not need a mentor to challenge his account of himself; he needs a comment section that agrees with him, and the algorithm is very good at finding him one.

What both groups are missing, underneath the very different content, is the same thing: adults who have committed to knowing them over time, who are positioned to say, gently or bluntly, that's not actually who you are, or that's not actually what manhood requires.
Formation is slow, repeated, and unglamorous in a way that content never is. It cannot be livestreamed because most of what it consists of is the boring, faithful showing-up that never trends.

t: The Third Column of Work
q: Hard Skills got you hired. Soft Skills got you promoted. The third column is Stake Skills. They keep you in the room.

You don't have to be a learning scientist to know what happens when that sentence enters the room. It does nothing. It has never worked, anywhere, one time. The boss doesn't care what drafted the thing.

This is taking that covered ass and turning it to face front. Same instinctual muscle. Same record that used to be in the shadows. But now you keep it on purpose, in the open, before anything goes wrong, instead of in secret for after it does.
A record only works when somebody has agreed to answer for it. I do below.
We all know producing got cheap. Answering for the thing did not. A machine can now fill column one (Hard Skills) faster than you ever could. It cannot touch column three (Stake Skills).
Find the one claim the whole thing rests on. The Big Idea, the number, the date, the quote, the line that would hurt most if wrong. Check that one claim against three unrelated sources.

t: The State Test Results Are In. And Four Minutes Suddenly Look a Lot Bigger.
q: If 7 x 8 requires a student to pause and figure it out, that costs something. If that same student is also trying to determine which operation to use, hold several numbers in working memory, interpret a word problem, decide what information matters, and make sense of the answer, the cost is much bigger.

When I look at the third-grade New York State math assessment data, overall state proficiency moved from 54% to 60%, then held steady at 60% -- a gain of 6 percentage points over three years, and a fairly steady climb. Our third grade moved from 67% to 57% to 88% -- a gain of 21 points, and nothing close to steady.

Take a look at the percentages at Level 4 (Exceeds): 7%, then 14%, then 41%. Forty-one percent of our third graders scored at the highest performance level on this year's state assessment -- a gain of 27 points in one school year.

For too long, I think we've treated fluency as a box students check before moving on -- they learned addition, then subtraction, then multiplication, then division, and if they didn't quite have it down, we kept moving anyway, because there was another standard, another unit, another lesson, another assessment on the calendar.

None of this cost the district anything extra. There was no new curriculum to purchase, no outside consultant, and no new professional development required. It was four minutes, carved out of a math block that already existed, taught by the teachers already in the room.

t: The Hidden Cost of Over-Responsibility (And What to Do About It)
q: This is not ambition gone wrong. It is a conditioned response. High performers learn early that stepping in gets results. When no one else moves, they move.

Team development stalls. When a leader consistently solves problems before team members have the opportunity to engage with them, those team members are being quietly deprived of the experiences that build competence, confidence, and ownership.
A meaningful pause is not a deep breath before a meeting. It is enough space for the physiological stress response to actually downregulate.
The third stage is right-resourcing. This is not offloading. It is identifying who or what actually owns this responsibility and executing a clean transfer.

The most common failure point here is a leader who makes an internal decision to step back and never tells the people who depend on the outcome. They remain implicitly responsible in everyone else's eyes, even after they have decided internally to let it go.
Because sustainable high performance is not about how much you can hold. It is about understanding your highest contribution clearly enough to protect the conditions that allow you to make it.

t: The Disappearance of Memorization -- And What We Lost
q: In an 1854 lecture at the University of Lille, French inventor Louis Pasteur famously said, in the fields of observation, chance favors only the prepared mind. In other words, scientific breakthroughs depend on a scientist's prior knowledge.
Sadly, very few students today memorize anything other than the multiplication table. Even forty years ago, memorization was on its way out.

In The Knowledge Deficit, E.D. Hirsch writes, The systematic acquisition of broad knowledge is precisely what it takes to become a good reader. He goes on to laud factual knowledge as well as the language it entails.

education researcher Daniel Willingham explains, research from cognitive science has shown that the sorts of skills that teachers want for students -- such as the ability to analyze and to think critically -- require extensive factual knowledge.

We are, at our core, remembering and story-making creatures, says Wilfred McClay in his American history textbook, Land of Hope. He continues, A culture without memory will necessarily be barbarous and easily tyrannized, even if it is technologically advanced.
Schools should bring back memorization. Students deserve to have rich, beautiful, informative, and culturally important knowledge in their mind's permanent collection.

t: The Desire Beneath the Ambition August 11, 2026
q: They wanted space to consider who they were becoming. How they wanted to lead. How they could do meaningful work without allowing the work to consume them.

How do I actually have a positive impact on our deeply challenged communities? How do I do good in the world while also creating a life for my family, my partner, and myself that allows for presence, joy, and peace?

And yet ambition can carry us far without ever telling us where we actually want to go. Along the way, it can become entangled with many things. Approval. Security. Proving ourselves. Money. Recognition.
We are rarely asked: When you show up in a room, what gets a little better because you are there? Said another way: What becomes more possible for others because you are here?
As I enter a new season of my own work, I am thinking less about how much more I can produce and more about what I most want my work to contribute.
I do know that the desire beneath my ambition has become clearer. I am not seeking simply to do more. I want what I do to help create a better life together.

t: Returning to Key Stage 3: Defining Curriculum Progression Before You Plan the Units
q: Topic-level sequencing is not the same thing as progression, and treating it as though it is one of the most common curriculum design errors I encounter.
Progression is not about topics getting harder. It's about a specific, nameable set of knowledge or skills getting stronger, more secure, more flexible, more transferable, across time.

If you cannot say precisely what is progressing, what specific thing a Year 9 student can do that a Year 7 student could not, beyond simply the topic being labeled more advanced, you do not actually have a progression model.
For each of those, write out what it looks like at a low level of security, a developing level, and a secure level. This becomes your progression model.
If you can't answer that for a given unit, the unit may still be worth teaching, but it should not be described as part of a progression model, because it isn't functioning as one.

t: Point, Shoot, Gone
q: When people photograph an object instead of simply observing it, they remember it less well than if they had just looked at it. The camera becomes a kind of cognitive offloading device.
Point, shoot, gone, the moment is captured but the memory of it is diminished.

This is speculative. I want to be honest that the direct research on AI-specific offloading and memory encoding is thin, and I am extrapolating from an adjacent, well-established literature rather than reporting a finding specific to AI use.

Passive receipt, read the output, move on, may function exactly like point-shoot-gone: the information now exists, captured, external, and the internal encoding work that would have created durable memory and understanding simply doesn't happen.
Close the chat window and explain the concept back in your own words, without looking. Generate three practice problems from the explanation you just received.
The AI did the retrieving or the generating. The student still has to do the encoding, and encoding is not a spectator activity.

t: People Do Not Do What You Say. They Do What You Reward
q: He did not say it as a complaint. He said it as a fact, the way you tell a visitor which way is north. And the thing that has stayed with me for twenty years is that he was right.
I cared about cash. I pushed it, raised it in meetings, argued it mattered. But I could see what actually got rewarded, and it was earnings. So I chased it.
The words said cash mattered. The attention said it did not. So did the money, since the incentives all paid out on earnings. And the organization was never confused about which signal to believe.
You cannot spend five years signaling that something does not matter and then act surprised when no one has been tending it.
It changed when the attention changed. The cash page stopped getting skipped. It moved up in the deck, ahead of earnings, so it was the first thing we looked at instead of the last thing we ignored.

t: No to typing: friction is learning
q: They knew the content. They knew how to answer the questions. But after around 18 months doing almost everything on laptops, many of them could no longer sustain handwriting at the speed the examination demanded.

Mueller and Oppenheimer's well-known 2014 study found that students taking notes by hand performed better on conceptual questions than students using laptops. Laptop users recorded more words and were more likely to reproduce lectures verbatim.
There is good reason to be cautious here. Subsequent attempts to replicate the original findings have produced much less decisive results.

Robert Bjork and Elizabeth Bjork describe the idea of desirable difficulties: conditions that can make performance feel harder in the short term while improving learning and retention over the longer term.
If I can type every word you say, I can capture without selecting. If I cannot keep up, I have to decide. And it's the deciding that requires thinking.
Every one of those tools can be useful. But each also removes a potential point at which the learner might previously have had to select, retrieve, organise, summarise or generate.

t: I'm Ambivalent About "The Science of Learning"
q: On the other side, I worry that the science of learning overpromises. Is there, truly, a science of learning? How much do we know about learning?

This is something I've found with a lot of effective teaching. It's not a generic strategy like break learning into small steps. Effective teaching is rooted in an understanding of the specific content to be taught.

There is nothing sacred about the normal curve. It is the distribution most appropriate to chance and random activity. Education is a purposeful activity and we seek to have the students learn what we have to teach.
I think that what Bloom called unsuccessful instruction is the norm. The bell curve is what most outcomes look like in education.
We know some stuff. We can describe a bit about the general shape of the thing that we might call the science of learning. But most of the specifics are yet to be filled in.
But the nitty-gritty practical knowledge that helps me put that stuff into practice in my classroom is full of lessons learned from trial and error, one part science and three parts empiricism.

t: Humans understand what AI cannot
q: Understanding is a Big Juicy Word, like justice or freedom, that is powerful and important yet perilous to define. No definition could possibly encompass the entirety of what we mean by understanding, yet we all have a general sense of it means.

It's knowledge of generalizations that can support procedural learning, and it's why procedural and conceptual knowledge have to happen in tandem. You can't first learn all the procedures and then learn the concepts later.

Dan Willingham describes understanding as remembering in disguise because it involves connecting new ideas to existing old ideas and then rearranging them -- making comparisons we hadn't made before, or thinking about a feature we previously ignored.
In contrast, large-language models at present are completely useless at this, in part because they lack any depth of understanding of what is happening in the minds of their users.
The program enables the person in the room to pass the Turing Test for understanding Chinese but he does not understand a word of Chinese.

As the cool stream gushed over one hand she spelled into the other the word water, first slowly, then rapidly. I stood still, my whole attention fixed upon the motions of her fingers. Suddenly I felt a misty consciousness as of something forgotten -- a thrill of returning thought; and somehow the mystery of language was revealed to me.
The living word awakened her soul -- what a beautiful testament to the power of human language to express human thought.

t: How Failure Labels Shape School Identity and Student Learning
q: Teachers and agencies like Ofsted, the Office for Standards in Education, who inspect schools in England, use labels as cognitive shortcuts. But what concerns me is that labels like requires improvement can change how people in those schools can negatively change how they think, behave, and interpret future information.

I've looked at schemes of work for lower ability sets and in almost all schools I've worked in, the pace of learning is slower, and students are expected to learn fewer topics than students in higher sets.

I've learned that once a student knows the label that they've been given by the school, they work hard to confirm that that label is true. It takes courage, resilience and perseverance to move past that label.
A few parents told me that because they weren't ever good at maths at school, they didn't expect their children to be able to grasp much maths even if it was well taught.

I like to replace labels with descriptions of behaviour so if a child I teach has been labelled as disruptive, I could watch how the disruptiveness struggles over a period of time and note that the student struggles with staying focused in afternoon lessons.

Labels work because people are always looking for ways to simplify the world, so a single word like lazy or bright or weak or gifted is a shortcut that shapes how students, teachers, parents and others view themselves.

t: Has the pendulum swung too far away from "college for all"?
q: But lately I've started to wonder whether we're overcorrecting, and whether the new consensus is quietly doing damage to a group of kids who don't fit either the old or the new story.

The data on selective four-year degrees, particularly in fields with real labor market demand, remain very strong. That has not changed. What has changed is the cultural permission structure around choosing that path.

A kid from a highly educated family who decides to skip college and become an electrician is making a choice from a position of security; college was always available to them, and they are opting out of it.
They are being nudged out of the option that had the best odds of changing their family's trajectory, potentially without ever being told clearly what the earnings data actually show.

But the current mood risks creating a new one-size-fits-all default, just pointed in the opposite direction, and it will do the most damage to exactly the kids who have the least other information to draw on.

It's the return of genuinely individualized guidance, the unglamorous, expensive, hard-to-scale work of a counselor or mentor who knows a specific kid well enough to say, for you, specifically... here is the path that gives you the best shot.

t: Good Leaders Explain How Failure Will Be Judged Before It Happens https://admiredleadership.com/good-leaders-explain-how-failure-will-be-judged-before-it-happens/
q: What separates resilient teams from fragile ones is not whether failure happens, but whether people understand, in advance, how that failure will be evaluated.

When the criteria for judging failure only become visible after the fact, people reasonably conclude that the standard is arbitrary, or worse, that it will be applied punitively depending on politics or mood.
A team that has never been told how failure will be judged learns, from a single incident, exactly one data point about their leader's true standards. That is a dangerous way to build trust.
If you follow the agreed process, disclose problems immediately, and ask for help when you need it, a bad outcome will not define how I see you.

People stop hiding problems because they know concealment, not failure itself, is what will actually be punished. They start asking for help earlier because they know that asking is rewarded, not treated as an admission of weakness.

The paradox is that clarifying how failure will be judged, before it happens, is one of the most effective ways to reduce the frequency and severity of failure itself, because it makes the early warning signs of failure something people surface rather than hide.

t: Goldman's CEO Told This Summer's Interns to Spar With the AI
q: He didn't tell them to avoid AI, and he didn't tell them to use it uncritically either. He told them to spar with it.
Spar implies engagement, not avoidance and not surrender. A boxer sparring with a partner isn't refusing to throw punches, and isn't just standing there absorbing them either.
Camp one wants students passively avoiding the tool. Camp two wants students passively deferring to it once they've learned to operate it. Sparring is neither.
Sparring requires the student to have enough of their own developing expertise to notice when the AI's output is off, and enough intellectual confidence to say so and push back.
The next required step is: find one thing in this output you think is wrong, incomplete, or could be argued with, and make that argument, with evidence, in your own words.
The discipline of actively hunting for the weak point in someone else's argument, even a very good one, is itself one of the most durable intellectual skills there is.

t: Don't Just Prepare Them to Use It. Prepare Them to Change It.
q: We are preparing an entire generation of students to be highly competent users of tools that other people built, for purposes other people decided, with values other people encoded, and we are calling that preparation for the future.
None of it gave a single student the ability to say, this recommendation algorithm is optimizing for engagement in a way that is harmful, and here is how I would build it differently.
If we only teach students to use AI tools well, we are training a generation of highly capable passengers.
They still don't know how to fly the plane, and more importantly, they have no say in where it goes.

It would mean giving students actual practice modifying, not just prompting, small models, seeing firsthand what happens when you change a training objective or a dataset, so the black box becomes at least partially a glass box.

But if we only ever prepare kids to be sophisticated passengers, we should not be surprised, twenty years from now, when they have exactly as much say over where AI takes society as this generation had over where social media took us.

t: Conflict Is Not the Problem, Silence Might Be
q: What they are actually doing, most of the time, is letting a known problem sit unaddressed because raising it feels harder than living with it.
It just moves the cost from a visible, contained conversation to a diffuse, ongoing tax on the whole team.
Conflict as performance, as venting, as a way to establish dominance, is genuinely corrosive, and leaders who mistake volume for honesty are not doing what I'm describing.
Most organizational silence isn't peaceful. It's just conflict that has gone underground, where it does more damage precisely because it's invisible to the people who could resolve it.
I think the actual skill leaders need is not conflict avoidance and it's not conflict-seeking. It's what I'd call conflict routing.
It's notice where a tension is currently leaking sideways, and move it, deliberately, into the one channel where it can be closed instead of just managed.

t: Bureaucrat SLAMS the Australian Education Research Organisation (AERO)
q: AERO's guidance materials, while individually well-researched, have become so voluminous and so procedurally hedged that classroom teachers often cannot actually locate a clear instructional recommendation inside them.

The organization exists because Australian education, for years, suffered from a research-to-practice gap, good evidence sitting in journals that teachers never read or could not easily translate into Monday morning lesson plans.

Guidance that is faithful to the evidence but so heavily qualified, so carefully hedged against every possible edge case and context variation, that a working teacher reading it at nine at night cannot extract a clear answer.
Hedging is not neutral, it has a cost, and the cost falls specifically on the practitioner who needed a usable answer and instead got several pages of caveats.
But hearing it from inside the system, from someone whose job depends on these documents functioning, lands differently than hearing it from outside critics like me.
It's that the translation layer between good research and usable classroom guidance is genuinely difficult to build well, even for an organization explicitly founded to build it.

t: Back to School: Between the First and Last Day of Class
q: The single biggest challenge we face is one of meaning: how do I know that my work is meaningful, that it actually bears fruit? This is the quandary of every teacher (and parent), and what amplifies the difficulty is the reality that human beings are changeable.
The curriculum is not messianic. Throughout history, how many villains have studied the same great works of literature and philosophy, and yet rejected noble pursuits?
We cannot force people to be better. We can and should limit acting out and misbehavior, but we do not control the heart of another.

Our foundation, then, is rather simple: we trust in the efficacy of ordinary means. What I mean by this is that we believe if we educate students in the right way, it will make a difference for them and ultimately for society.
We don't prejudge our students, colleagues, or parents. We let their actions and words speak for themselves. When something makes us wonder, we ask about it.

The difference you will make cannot be measured today, or tomorrow, or even next year. In fact, I'm not sure it can ever be measured in exactly a way that would satisfy us; that would give us undeniable evidence of success.

t: AI can do lots of things... but should it?
q: I've been sitting with a distinction lately that I don't think gets made often enough in conversations about AI and learning: the gap between what AI can do and what it should do, given what we actually know about how people learn.
AI can generate a complete, polished essay outline in four seconds. Should a student who is still learning how to structure an argument receive that outline before attempting their own? Probably not.

A vendor can show you, in ninety seconds, that their tool can do something impressive. Almost no vendor demo includes should we be giving students this at this moment in their learning, because that question doesn't sell software.
Does providing this capability, right now, to this student, at this point in their learning, support or bypass the specific cognitive work this task is meant to build.
At that point the struggle has already happened, and the tool is adding value rather than removing necessary difficulty.

That is a judgment call about timing and sequencing that has to be made deliberately, task by task, student by student, and it is exactly the judgment call that gets skipped when the operating question is only can it do this.

t: A System Prompt for K-12
q: The STUDENTS FIRST Act is this kind of text. Every provision reallocates permissions inside the existing operating logic of school. Grading, seat time, standardized assessment, discipline pathways, and credentialing all remain in place.

Students are watching teachers cede knowledge and agency to AI tools in ways that erode instruction and connection. They are receiving AI slop as instructional material. They saw a specific failure mode in the system they inhabit and wrote a mitigation into the prompt.
System prompts get outranked. Later instructions override them. Base model defaults override them. Tools with their own permissions override them.
The detector and lockdown browser requirements in Section 4.2 will survive. Districts already own the surveillance infrastructure.
No district has a process for genuine consultation, and none has an incentive to build one. Most districts finalize policy in August.

But the STUDENTS FIRST Act does not offer a clear pathway for creating such a loop. Interested districts will read it, engage with selected parts, ignore others, and the students who wrote it will have no way to learn what districts actually did or to press for revisions.

t: "I Know It When I See It" Doesn't Scale
q: Humans are surprisingly good at compensating for vague instructions. Or at least trying to. They fill in gaps. They infer what you probably meant. They learn your preferences over time. AI is much less forgiving.
She couldn't just tell the AI, Make this better. She had to explain what better meant.
The most interesting thing here isn't that she built an AI-writing tool that her team could use; it's that using AI forced her to make something explicit that had always been implicit.
If the only way your team can produce great work is by routing everything through you, then you haven't scaled your judgment. You've just made yourself the bottleneck.

Most of us carry around a lot of tacit knowledge. We know a presentation feels too long or when an email buries the lead or when something isn't quite right. But often, we don't know how to explain why, and no one has ever forced us to.
Ironically, AI may end up making us better managers because it forces us to do something we should have been doing all along: making our judgment visible.

t: "Everyone felt like we were supporting and building together": An Interview, Part 2
q: We never let it become a place where people demoed their AI tool of the week and everyone clapped. That's the default gravity of these groups, and if you don't fight it deliberately, that's what you get.
Every session had to include at least one person saying something that didn't work, a failed prompt, a bad outcome with students, an assignment redesign that flopped.

There was a period, maybe eight months in, where a couple of the loudest voices in the room started treating it like a debate club, arguing AI-maximalist versus AI-skeptic positions at each other, and everyone else just went quiet.
I emailed six people who'd gone quiet and just asked, one on one, what's actually going on for you right now with this. Their answers had almost nothing to do with the debate happening in the group.

The actual value, especially early, is just building enough trust that people will say the true, unglamorous version of what's happening in their classroom instead of the version they think they're supposed to say.
Everyone felt like we were supporting and building together, not like we were being trained or evaluated. That distinction is basically the whole thing.

t: Why You Lose Patience Even When You Care
q: The problem is not always that you need better parenting advice. Sometimes stress has made that advice temporarily unavailable.

The difficulty is not always knowing what good parenting looks like. The difficulty is accessing it while the shoes are still missing, the child is yelling, the baby has just woken up, and you are already late.
Caring does not create endless capacity. Love does not erase fatigue. Understanding your child's needs does not guarantee that your body can remain flexible under every condition.

A parent can say, "I understand that you're upset," while communicating, through every other signal, "Your upset is unbearable, and I need it to stop immediately." Children are often more responsive to the second message.
What began as an attempt to guide the child becomes an attempt to end the parent's own discomfort. That shift tends to make responses bigger.
Stay calm" is not especially useful advice when you are already overwhelmed. It can sound like one more standard you have failed to meet.
Your child's behavior is not the only thing shaping the interaction. Your nervous system is part of the environment, too. That is not a reason for blame. It is a source of leverage.

t: Why Some Conversations Don't Need a Script
q: There's a small set of things a teacher can say — not content, just moves — that turn a flat discussion into a real one. Say more about that. Who can put that in their own words? Do you agree or disagree, and why?
They worked with adults almost exactly the way they worked with fourteen-year-olds, which surprised me more than it should have.

Conversation should be harder than giving a speech. You can't plan ahead, since you don't know what the other person will say. And yet none of this makes conversation feel hard. It's speeches that feel hard.
Multiply that across a whole conversation, and two people's language starts drifting toward each other without either one deciding to make that happen.
Two people who keep converging on the same language end up, almost as a side effect, converging on the same understanding of the situation.

Alignment happens fastest when trust is high and people are genuinely listening. It happens more slowly, or gets blocked, in rooms where people are guarded, where there's history, or where one person's job is technically to evaluate the other.
Not a paraphrase. Not "so what you're saying is." Just their exact words, echoed, followed by a pause or a follow-up question.
Most people, once they hear their own words handed back to them, will expand on the idea or correct it if you got it slightly wrong.

t: Weaponising NAPLAN: How Underachievement Is Being Used to Indict Explicit Instruction
q: The short story on NAPLAN is that it shows a persisting pattern of under-achievement in literacy and numeracy by about a third of Australian students.
To put this into real terms 132,857 of the 1.3 million children in Years 3, 5, 7 and 9 not keeping up with basic classroom learning.

In schools across the country that have used explicit teaching methods for a while, what's sometimes called phonics, and small group tutoring, where you give kids who are struggling extra intensive help, we are seeing big leaps.
In plain terms, the 2026 NAPLAN results cannot possibly tell us anything about the impact of statewide pushes for explicit instruction. Takes a little longer than that to turn a ship one would think.
Four years ago, testing at Djidi Djidi Aboriginal School revealed 16 of the 18 students in years 5 and 6 were at or below year 3 level in literacy.
If we were sending 100 kids to high school, 90 of them couldn't read or write as per their age — and that's failing those students.
All you can tell from a standardised test is a kid's postal code
More advantaged students will tend to be academically successful despite the choices we make, whereas the performance of less advantaged students is more likely to be because of what we've done

t: Trust Is Contagious, or Why Trust Exercises at Offsites Are So Important
q: Researchers reviewing 21 studies involving more than 11,000 people found that a single interaction changes how willing people are to trust a completely different person.
One recent experience with someone trustworthy is enough to shift the baseline. In fact, after just one such interaction, people even overestimate how likely others are to prove trustworthy as well.
The reverse also holds true. After a betrayal, people become more suspicious of others who had nothing to do with it.
One person's broken promise can make everyone a little warier. One person's follow-through can make the whole team a little more willing to take a risk on one another.

Wise leaders use offsites, team meetings, and learning experiences to fill the team with demonstrations of trust. They don't do this for fun. They do it to create low-stakes situations where trust can be extended and rewarded.
The specific activity matters less than the structure and payoff: Team members extend trust, others honor it, and the whole room absorbs the result.
Good leaders don't wait for trust to develop on its own. They build the moments and experiences that produce it.

t: The Three Stages of Emigration Grief: An Academic's Guide to Learning the Australian Education System
q: My experience of adjusting to Australian education and teacher education has broadly involved three stages: honeymoon, devastation and confusion, and finally, pragmatism and hope.
AITSL, NESA, VIT, QCT, APST, LANTITE — they seem less like an administrative obstacle and more like an interesting new dialect of a language you already speak.
The first shock is not that you know nothing. It is that you know quite a lot, but not necessarily the right things.
The temptation to compare is enormous because comparison is how we make the unfamiliar intelligible. Unfortunately, it can also become a trap.
In Australia, you may understand the published policy perfectly well while missing the twenty years of history sitting invisibly behind it. Everyone else hears the subtext; you hear the sentence.
You stop asking, "What is the English equivalent?" and start asking, "How does this work here, and why?" That small shift changes everything.
You stop trying to recreate the professional world you left behind and start contributing to the one you are now part of.

t: The Next Compact
q: America rewrites its deal with college roughly once a generation. The last rewrite was fifty years ago. Everyone is now fighting over the corpse of the old one — and nobody is drafting the new one.
a diploma should stop being a receipt and become a warrant. We watched her do it. We challenged her on it. We are staking our name on her.

Fifty-two percent of four-year graduates are underemployed a year after graduation. For the first time in the modern record, recent college graduates have a higher unemployment rate than the workforce as a whole.

Stanford's Digital Economy Lab found that employment for 22-to-25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed occupations has dropped roughly 13-16% since late 2022, while older workers in the same jobs held steady.

What's scarce is proof. Proof that a human being can actually do what their credential claims. Proof that an institution's promises mean something. The old compact traded access for money. The next compact must trade proof for trust.
Registered apprenticeships have doubled in a decade to 680,000 — a start, and still a rounding error against 15 million undergraduates.
Incumbents have never written the next compact. A shopkeeper's son wrote the land-grant deal. The American Legion drafted the GI Bill. Governors invented WGU.

t: The Main Work of Your Marriage
q: You are called to shepherd your wife. You are the leader. You are the protector. This will look different depending on the type of woman you marry.

Is the woman brash and outspoken? Your primary work will be to help her cultivate a gentle, quiet spirit. Is the woman timid and complacent? Your primary work will be to pull her out of her shell and nurture the habit of hospitality.
Here's the important thing to keep in mind: you're not perfect either. Have some humility. But it is not your wife's responsibility to make you a better person. That's your responsibility, too.

You can't teach financial discipline, for example, if you don't have financial discipline. A man who buys whatever he wants regardless of the consequences, yet locks down his wife's allowance to a paltry sum, is a despot suited for the third world, not a loving home.
Your future wife should complement you. She should be strong where you are weak. Together, you two should be able to accomplish much more than if you were apart.
Husbands, live with your wives in an understanding way, showing honor to the woman as the weaker vessel, since they are heirs with you of the grace of life.

t: The Cracked Sidewalk
q: Concrete is extraordinarily strong in compression and comparatively weak in tension. A great deal of craft goes into influencing the outcome. Each decision reduces uncertainty. None repeals physics.

When tensile stress eventually exceeds what the concrete can accommodate, the slab cracks. If the joint has done its work, the fracture forms beneath the groove, where the irregular break is concealed within a straight, deliberately placed line. What looks like decoration is, in part, managed fracture.
Yet engineering does this routinely because maximum strength at every individual point is not the same thing as resilience of the whole.
A sufficiently well-managed organization is sometimes expected to eliminate such conditions. That expectation is roughly equivalent to specifying concrete that will never shrink.

A quality failure produces a new procedure. A missed target produces another reporting requirement. An accident produces retraining. The visible opening disappears. Sometimes the repair is correct. Sometimes someone has simply poured filler into an instrument.

If reporting channels existed, why did the information travel around them? If inspections existed, why was the defect discovered elsewhere? If people were authorized to raise concerns, why did they wait?
The contraction joints record what the designer expected. The cracks record what actually happened. The distance between those two is where the interesting work begins.

t: The Best Thing You Can Do Before the School Year Starts Has Nothing to Do With Curriculum
q: Somewhere underneath all of that is a question you probably haven't said out loud: What if I don't know enough to do this well?
Even though I believed strongly in project based and experiential learning, I had bought into the idea that the right materials would do the work.
Your kids don't read your lesson plans. They read you. They notice whether you find something genuinely interesting or whether you're pushing through it because it's on the schedule.
That dread was mine. My kids didn't come with it. But I was handing it to them anyway.
Grammar as its own subject wasn't working. Grammar in the service of a story she actually cared about? Completely different.
You start to catch yourself sooner — when the resistance in the room is coming from your kid, and when it's coming from you.
The parents who do this well aren't the ones who knew the most at the start. They're the ones who stayed open to learning on the job.
The best preparation you can do this August has nothing to do with curriculum. It's deciding to be a learner yourself — right alongside your kid, from day one.

t: The Best Leadership Reading List: July 2026
q: Welcome to our country's emerging "forever-tight" labor market. What will this require of you, the employer? Since the underlying cause of this relentless tightening of labor supply is structural, it is likely that your own organization—whether for-profit, nonprofit, or governmental—will in turn be forced to undertake comparable structural changes in how you find, hire, and retain your workers.

Constant availability generates constant urgency. The result is a relentless "hurry, hurry, hurry" mindset that leaves little room for anything but reaction—an exhausting and unsustainable place to lead from.
To influence an organization of any meaningful size, even a team of ten, you need to understand the realities of how work actually gets done. High-level strategy alone rarely changes behavior.
The machine is spinning faster than they can process and think. The acceleration extends far beyond AI: the inbox, the KPIs, escalating disruptions, tools meant to save time that consume more.
They ask concrete questions rather than open evaluative ones. "Walk me through what you decided this week," produces a different conversation than "How are things?
Leadership is not about ownership. It is about stewardship—leaving people, institutions, and communities stronger for the next generation.
It is often better to preface a question with a confession of some sort, or with information from yourself. That sets a standard for the respondent. Set that standard high!
And the number one thing that comes back for the successful implementations is, hey, did you know what problem you were trying to solve to begin with?

t: The Art of Being Present
q: It's entirely possible to be sitting beside a swimming pool while mentally rehearsing next week's presentation. To be building sandcastles with your children while replying to emails in your head.
Being present is about giving your brain permission to experience what's actually happening instead of constantly predicting, planning or problem solving.

You don't need to meditate for an hour every morning or empty your mind. You simply need to notice when your attention has wandered and gently bring it back. Again. And again. And again. Presence isn't perfection. It's returning.
Somatic intelligence is our ability to notice the physical sensations that accompany our thoughts and emotions, and use them as information rather than ignoring them.
Maybe your stomach drops before opening your inbox, even when you're technically on holiday. Those sensations can be clues.

The more we practise being present while playing with our children, sharing a meal with friends or walking the dog, the easier it becomes to bring that same presence into the workplace. We listen more carefully. We notice more. We connect better.
The greatest gift we can give someone isn't always our advice or our expertise, sometimes it's our full attention.

t: The Abilene Paradox: Why Your Team Agreed to a Plan Nobody Wanted
q: Over the next few days after that decision, in separate 1:1s, three different people on my team told me that they weren't quite sure about the timeline. All of them were in the meeting, but not one of them had said a word in the room.
And that's how a team of smart, honest people ends up committing to a plan that, individually, none of them wanted. This was an example of the Abilene Paradox in action.
When a group agrees to do something that nobody in the group actually wants, because everyone assumes they're the only one who is not into it.

The most subtle, and dangerous, part of the Abilene Paradox is this: nobody in the room is being dishonest or spineless. Each person is making a reasonable decision based on the wrong assumption about what everyone else believes.
Groupthink is what happens when a group actively suppresses real dissent to protect harmony. Someone in the room has a real, strong objection.

It's closer to "I have a nagging feeling, but everyone else looks fine, so it's probably just me." The fix in this case is making everyone's private hesitation visible to everyone else at the same time, before the group locks in on the wrong direction.
This is what makes the Abilene Paradox dangerous. A team can have excellent psychological safety, yet still run into the trap of the paradox.

t: Scaling Is Not Copy-Paste
q: Most organizations say they want to scale. They do not. They want to replicate. They want to find the thing that worked in one place, copy it, paste it somewhere else, and get the same result without having to re-learn all the messy local conditions that made it work the first time.
Scaling means the district identifies the underlying conditions that made the practice work. Then each school builds a version that fits its size, schedule, leadership capacity, and current culture.

We blame people for "not implementing with fidelity" when we never actually figured out whether the thing needed fidelity or adaptation. We blame schools for "resisting change" when we handed them a solution built for someone else's problem.
You cannot scale meaningful work by eliminating judgment. You scale meaningful work by developing judgment.
Application is: Use the idea. Replication is: Preserve the model. Scaling is: Protect the essence while adapting the form.
Most failed initiatives give people a thing to replicate, call it scaling, offer training designed for application, and then wonder why implementation is inconsistent.

t: My Summer With the Humanities and What It Taught Me About Ausubel's Meaningful Learning
q: Traditionally, I would build my content knowledge specific to the content I teach for my grade level. For example, when I taught second grade, I focused on building my knowledge of Ancient Greece, Ancient China, Ancient India.

It took that knowledge I had acquired over several years, which had been somewhat isolated bits of knowledge, and connected it all into one schema. It made that knowledge stronger and deeper, and gave me a better picture of the ancient world as a whole.

Through my own summer learning experience, I realized that I need to intentionally design my lessons to build and strengthen connections between knowledge my students learned in earlier grades and what they will learn this year.
Their knowledge of each civilization is isolated, and they are unaware of the connections across the content. This also increases the likelihood they will forget what they have learned.

Intentionally review content they have learned in earlier grades. Explicitly connect third grade content to content learned in earlier grades. Design learning experiences that advance students towards the generalization and adaptation phases of the instructional hierarchy so they can build connections across content.

t: Making Sense of Self Doubt: "What if I Am Wrong?"
q: What if I'm wrong, and everyone in the room can see it except me?" I remember sitting in a meeting room, there were too many people I didn't know well and few senior people for me to be comfortable.
The conversation moved on without me making a point, and I felt disappointment and relief at the same time.
Everyone, somewhere in the org chart, is convinced the right answer is sitting in someone else's office.
Leadership rarely means seeing the truth before everyone else does. More often it means being willing to offer an interpretation that wasn't articulated yet.

The organisational researcher Karl Weick suggests you don't know what you think until you see what you said. Certainty isn't reliably the thing that comes before you speak, it shows up after we speak, or it could not show up at all.
The first says, "I call them as they are". He believes there's an objective, measurable truth out there, and his job is simply to register it.

Most of us move through work assuming we're the first umpire, waiting to register a truth that already exists, if only we look hard enough or wait long enough. But most of the moments that matter at work, the ones where people are looking to you for a read, are closer to the third. Nothing is decided until someone decides it.

t: LinkedIn's Top Colleges, Workers' GDP Share Hits Record Low, and KPMG Interns Eye the C-Suite
q: LinkedIn ranked the 50 U.S. colleges that best set graduates up for long-term career success, with Princeton leading the list for the second year in a row.
Families are no longer just asking, "What is the most prestigious school?" They are asking, "What does this school actually help you do after graduation?
According to Bureau of Labor Statistics data cited by Reuters, labor's share of nominal GDP fell to 52.9% in the second quarter, down from 53.7% in the first quarter.
If productivity rises and employees do not feel any meaningful improvement in pay, opportunity, workload, flexibility, or career growth, the productivity story becomes a trust problem.
Nearly all respondents, 93%, said they aspire to reach the C-suite or senior executive roles during their careers.
76% said long-term success will require both strong human skills and the ability to direct AI agents effectively.
Parents calling employers crosses a line, but it also says something about the pressure young workers are under.

t: Is It Okay for Parents to Use AI to Advocate for Their Kids?
q: So many parents still see AI, or ChatGPT more specifically, as a tool students use to cheat, or they have conscientious objections to it. There's this very binary thinking surrounding it. It's either all good or all bad, with nothing in between.

Connecticut saw a 29.6% increase in special education complaint filings from 2023-24 to 2024-25. Experts say increased understanding of special education law may be contributing to the increase, and some specifically point to parents' use of AI.
Think about what parents can do now when they have a resource that can help them with that: how to understand the laws, figure out what questions to ask, and help them actually write the letters.

Financial aid offices are now complaining that the growing number of appeals is creating an incredible workflow problem because more students and parents are submitting them with the help of tools like ChatGPT.
I think it's pretty safe to say that the AI ship of hoping students and parents stop using it has sailed so far over the horizon you can't even see it anymore.
According to a recent survey, more than 50% of parents are now using AI to help them decide which colleges to send their kids to.

t: How to Make Good Habits Easy and Bad Habits Hard
q: You think you have a discipline problem. You probably don't. You have a habit of making the wrong thing easier.
There is always a gap between: "I should do this." and "I am doing this." That gap is friction.
Instead of asking: "How do I force myself to do this?" Ask: "Why is this harder to start than it needs to be?
You're making a decision today that your future self won't have to make. That's proactive laziness. And honestly? That's a good thing.
Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein call this broader idea choice architecture: the way choices are arranged can influence what people actually choose.
Your environment doesn't care about your goals. It will make whatever is convenient easier. So make convenience work for you.
The disciplined version of you wasn't hiding somewhere inside you waiting to emerge. You built them. One tiny environmental decision at a time.

t: How To Show Hospitality When You Live in a Small Home
q: Housing in my area and many others has gotten far more expensive over the years, and I have known many people who have become "house poor" by continually upsizing. Yet my family and many others can attest that it is possible to live contentedly in a relatively small home.
Just the other day we had 10 people for dinner, which means the table stretched from the wall of the dining room all the way into the living room. It was tight, but that's okay. We're used to it.
We understood this to be the Lord's provision for us and never wanted to be ashamed of what he provided.
When you have more guests than your home can hold, ask nearby friends whether they can host the overflow. There's no reason that hospitality can't become a community project!

No one ever said hospitality would be easy and, in fact, I'm quite sure that the difficulty is part of the point of it. There's a reason that Peter says "show hospitality to one another without grumbling" (1 Peter 4:9).
It is not actually your home, but the Lord's. He has simply entrusted it to you and now holds you responsible for using it well.
A small home may limit some of the ways you do this, but it must not prevent you from doing so altogether.

t: How Dickhead Decisions Turn Ordinary People into Dicks
q: A dickhead decision gets made. Then people become dicks trying to make reality conform to it.

Some systems can absorb the embarrassment of being wrong. They reconsider assumptions, revise targets, alter course, and learn. Others protect the original decision. That is when an ordinary error starts becoming a dickhead decision.
Their intelligence helped them make sense of the world that produced their success. Dickheadedness begins when they continue imposing that understanding on a world that has moved on.

Those who support it are positive, ambitious, strategic, resilient, commercial. Those who question it are negative, resistant, tactical, cautious, stuck in the past. Evidence has quietly become morality.
Aggression becomes decisiveness. Detachment becomes professionalism. Intimidation becomes accountability. Denial becomes resilience. Manipulation becomes getting things done.
