The institution asks people to distrust their own judgment while holding them accountable for demonstrating conviction. Self-betrayal becomes a professional competence.
Teaching people to endure a dickhead system more effectively can increase the durability of the dickhead system.
And perhaps most importantly: What happens to someone who says, early and clearly, "I think we may have got this wrong"?

t: Feedback Is Not a Feature
q: There was no prior dialogue with this senior leader. No indication that anything could be the matter. No warning. She was telling me I needed to be a better "team player"; examples of how I failed at this were absent.
Feedback is often treated as just a communication skill. It isn't. It's a relational outcome.

Even the most well-structured feedback will fail if trust has not been established. A person's reptilian brain can easily fall into the trap of questioning feedback as genuine or a criticism, activating a sense of threat. A threatened brain doesn't parse feedback. It just braces.
People are not inherently bad at giving feedback. They do not know how to execute on the key elements that make it heard.
An AI thought partner can help here too, not to generate the feedback, but to decode it.
Feedback isn't a feature you bolt on when things go sideways. It's infrastructure. And infrastructure has to exist before you can run anything through it.
What most people miss is that feedback isn't judged by what was said. It's judged by what was already true between two people when it was said.

t: Connecting the Dots: A Series on Multi-Tiered System of Supports (MTSS) at My School — Tiers 2 and 3
q: A multi-tiered system of supports framework is designed to provide layers of intensified support for students who are not responding to explicit and systematic core instruction.

What ends up happening is that any student who receives intervention from a reading interventionist is identified as receiving Tier 3 support. Often, we start students with the heaviest amount of support, such as 5 days a week for 30 minutes of intervention with an integrated program like UFLI, Phonics for Reading, EBLI, and other intervention programs.

A student who can read some connected text at the beginning of first grade is very different from a student who can not read any words at all. At my school, these two students might land in the same intervention group, both labeled as receiving Tier 3 supports and the same intervention.

This student is a 5th grader who is reading with 53% accuracy and only 10 words at the beginning of 5th grade. This student might require increased dosage, but when too many students qualify for interventions, interventionists in a school setting can rarely dedicate additional periods to provide intensified instruction for this student.

It is unfair to expect students to go from intensive 5 day a week interventions to little to no support at all. A team of educators should be responsible for carefully and intentionally planning how supports are faded and whether a student is successful once supports are removed.

If students can maintain their success and data reflects progress, teams should proceed with exiting the student. If the student begins to regress or needs more support, teams should be ready to reinstall their intervention support.

t: Beware the EdTech Industry Rebrand: Part 2
q: The backlash to EdTech is not actually about "screentime" (too much vs. too little). The backlash is in response to the fact that the business model of Big Tech and EdTech companies is in direct conflict with healthy child development.

First, ISTE considers Google and Meta both proud funding sponsors and partners. That alone should stop anyone genuinely concerned about children's use of such products from reading the rest of the document.

Our finding that students across all skill levels perform more poorly on a digital test than on paper, is an urgent call for a more nuanced perspective on implementation of digital technologies in elementary education, and a signal to policy makers, school administrators and educators that the medium matters, especially for reading comprehension.

A troubling divide is emerging: mass, app-based instruction for the many, and human tutoring and intellectual exchange reserved for the elite. What is sold as the 'democratisation' of education may be entrenching further inequality.

Looking deeper into Instructure's report we see that only 40% of what they deem as the "top EdTech tools" they analyzed have any level of ESSA evidence and even worse, the majority have only Tier 3 which describes research that shows "promising evidence" and Tier 4 isn't even research - it's a rationale!
This "groundbreaking $23 million education initiative" will provide access to "free AI training and curriculum for all 1.8 million members of the AFT, starting with K-12 educators.

These companies are worried, as evidenced by the hate mail and death threats we've both gotten for speaking up and out about this. But it's because they know we are right, and they see the pushback growing from all over the world.

t: AI Is Quietly Changing Who Gets to Build Software
q: Frontier models can be amazingly proficient in one category (coding) and completely unimpressive in many others (writing, social reasoning, etc.). Knowing the difference matters.

Breen used a combination of OpenAI's GPT 5.6 and Claude's Fable to create a searchable database of prize-winning and nominated nonfiction. Breen argues that reading quality non-fiction books are the antithesis of AI slop, but it has become really hard to find exceptional writing authored by human beings.
Using AI code, we no longer have to rely on a vendor to provide us with a digital product. We can now create those experiences, edit them, take ownership of them, and respond in real time.
Tasking Codex or Claude Code to complete a project is increasingly voyeuristic—you watch a machine do the work and wait for it to finish.
For a few dollars a month, anyone can task their AI coding agent to rewrite text hundreds of times, testing it against Pangram's classifier until it passes detection.

A high school teacher working in the poorest district in the United States has greater access to premium AI tools, coupled with data protection, than a professor working at some of the wealthier universities.

While some K12 districts have started mandating teachers use AI tools in their classrooms, no college campus has been so instructive or intrusive to telling its faculty to do so, leaving individual instructors to decide what response to AI in their class is appropriate.

t: 383. The Zoo I Built
q: There is no better teammate at 8am on a Monday. There is also no worse teammate at 8am on a Monday, because the Dog can't tell a real threat from the mailman.
The problem is you can't get the Cat to do anything the Cat didn't already decide to do on her own. I said I wanted someone independent. I probably should have been more specific.
I'm seeing incredible opportunities on the horizon," says the Giraffe, while eleven feet below, the building is on fire, payroll didn't go out, and two engineers just quit.

You had an idea last Tuesday. Two days later, the Raccoon presents the exact same idea in the all-hands meeting. He had washed it off, polished it up, and delivered it with total confidence and zero indication of where it came from.
Umm...We tried that in 2019 and it didn't work." That's it. That's the whole contribution from the Elephant.
I didn't just hire these traits, I promoted the exact traits that now drive me crazy. A zoo takes after its keeper. The team is anxious because I'm anxious.
The best leaders aren't necessarily a particular animal. They're the ones who can sense which animal they're being, and pick a better one when it matters.

t: researchED Melbourne Returns
q: As we all sat in a large space on the ninth floor, he reminded us that Haileybury was a pioneer of explicit teaching, first trialling it in 2007/8.

Although a genuine matter of concern, I do find it interesting that this is one of five NAPLAN outcomes, with girls outperforming boys on the other four.

I am nervous about applying uniform models of learning in a school, especially a universal lesson plan structure -- which is how it seemed the Instructional Hierarchy was being interpreted in this case.

I remember that for several years, the English teachers at my school were unsure whether mini whiteboards had anything to offer their subject. Eventually, with the help of resources such as Doug Lemov's Teach Like a Champion videos, they began to experiment and took ownership of mini whiteboards for themselves.

t: Why These Subjects?
q: My answer is not that everyone independently discovered the same canon, but the same educational problems seem to reappear in education.

Aaron Benavot and colleagues, experts in comparative studies in education, examined official primary curricula worldwide from 1920 to 1986. Across very disparate countries, rich and poor, the subject categories and the shares of the week given to them converged.

Language, mathematics, science, and history do unusually generative work because knowledge in each helps a student acquire and judge knowledge elsewhere, as well as helps to organize a larger body of knowledge and skills.

It was not true. The curriculum kept subject teaching and required each school to run at least one multidisciplinary learning module a year, with assessment inside those modules still tied to the objectives of the participating subjects.

AI makes the value of this knowledge more visible and less likely to be attained. It can produce a polished answer that is incomplete or wrong. Knowledge helps users notice errors, question conclusions, and check sources.
A school that answers a biased canon by teaching less has only ensured that fewer children have anything to argue with.

t: Why Learn to Write in the Age of AI?
q: Schools often treat writing as the final step of learning: first you understand it, then you write it up. But in practice, writing is often the very thing that creates understanding.
So if a teenager asked me why they should bother to learn to write in the age of AI, I would tell them this: writing is thinking.

When you write about a topic from memory, you're forced to pull information out of your head rather than simply recognize it on a page. This kind of active retrieval strengthens memory significantly more than simply rereading or highlighting.

Psychologists have shown that most of us walk around with an "illusion of explanatory depth", which means that we feel like we understand things far better than we actually do, until we're asked to explain them.

Desirable difficulty, which describes conditions that slow learning down in the moment but make it stick far better in the long run, is the underlying idea behind all of these learning science concepts.

One study of a ten-week creative writing program found that students' critical thinking scores rose 25% while a matched control group barely moved, and other creative writing interventions have produced measurable gains in cognitive flexibility.
The first two levels of Depth of Knowledge (recall and recognition) are increasingly easy to outsource, since AI can summarize, restate, and recombine information quickly.

t: Weekly Reading Rundown - What People Have Been Writing This Week
q: Just sharing some posts I have enjoyed reading that have inspired me, made me think deeply or made me laugh.

Mary Myatt writes about the comfort a precise-looking number often gives us. Her distinction between precision and accuracy is spot on: a grade can look exact while hiding differences in task difficulty, marking and curriculum content.
Carl Hendrick argues that retrieval practice needs to be planned through the curriculum, with deliberate routes back to earlier knowledge.

Adam Boxer poses the idea that schools to need to strengthen universal provision before reaching for labels, reduced curricula or separate interventions when a pupil is struggling. He suggests that real inclusion is rarely so neat.
Robert Pondiscio introduces The Practice Project, a collaboration between AEI and researchED that aims to turn education research into professional knowledge teachers can use.
Eric Hudson goes beyond the usual list of AI tools and asks schools to examine the choices behind them. He looks at devices, student agency, AI policies and infrastructure.
Mark Fraser shares a practical way to judge whether technology has removed unnecessary difficulty or removed the work through which learning happens.
If you have found an excellent free education post on Substack, send me the link. I'll read the whole thing before I recommend it.

t: The War for the Human Soul: Five Lessons from C.S. Lewis's Space Trilogy
q: Lewis wrote the Space Trilogy between 1938 and 1945, in the middle of WWII, and it's quite impressive how he managed to predict so accurately what our very own postmodern ideological landscape would look like.

Masterfully, Lewis reminds us that our world is a fallen one, in which fighting will always be a necessity. This is an important reminder for us, because forgetting the truth of the earth as a battleground will make us more liable to fall into nihilism, despair, or pleasure-seeking.
The lesson for us then, is that discomfort, resistance, and cultural hostility are the expected conditions of a fallen world in which we've chosen to reject God.
The N.I.C.E. is Lewis's portrait of institutional evil, as a bureaucratic, well-funded, and respectable entity that claims to seek progress, science, and the betterment of mankind.

His education had been neither scientific nor classical--merely "Modern." The severities both of abstraction and of high human tradition had passed him by: and he had neither peasant shrewdness nor aristocratic honour to help him.

Isn't it absolutely essential to keep a fierce Left and fierce Right, both on their toes and each terrified of the other? That's how we get things done. Any opposition to the NICE is represented as a Left racket in the Right papers and a Right racket in the Left papers.

A man who cannot recognize the spirit of the N.I.C.E. in its contemporary forms (corporations, universities, media organizations, cultural movements, Hollywood), is a man who will serve it without ever knowing what he's doing or understanding why it's wrong.

t: The Truth About People Pleasing
q: The root of chronic people pleasing is not concern for others. It's concern for their acceptance and approval.

Psychologists find that what underlies people pleasing is the fear of being disliked and rejected. When we bend over backward to accommodate others at the expense of our own needs, it's because we depend on them for self-esteem.
Every time I failed to tell a driver that the car felt like Antarctica, I was setting another passenger up to shiver.
People pleasing is based on insecure attachment. We become people pleasers when we discover that others only value us when we're cooperative to the point of being submissive and deferential.
We shouldn't mistake the past origin of a behavior pattern for the current purpose it serves. A fear of being disliked leads too many of us to put our image above our values.
Sharing your preferences is not a display of disrespect. It's an expression of self-respect.

t: The Tragedy of the Accelerator
q: My colleagues all did things differently - because each served a different product team, with different goals and different needs. Each product team set its own priorities, which drove my colleagues' decision-making.

How hard would it be, I wondered aloud, to cancel the contract for the vendor he'd chosen? It would be so much easier to just use this existing platform, as-is, instead of trying to mold an unrelated system to our needs.

I was starting to fully understand the term I'd learned in grad school: sunk cost fallacy. We'd already put so much time, effort, and money into The Aggravator - but did what we'd already spent justify spending even more?

If the leader is certain, you should be certain, too. Or at least willing to suspend your own doubts in favor of what that leader deems to be true. As I learned the hard way, secondhand certainty only goes so far.
A new leader was swiftly appointed. He took stock of what our team was doing and made some changes. He didn't slow down the Accelerator project - he killed it.
But if someone had point-blank asked me why we needed this platform, my only true answer would have been, "Because Dave said so.

t: The Idea That Refused to Die: Part 1: From Bartlett to the Cognitive 'Revolution'
q: In his 1932 book Remembering: A Study in Experimental and Social Psychology, Frederic Bartlett first introduced the notion of cognitive schemas (or schemata), a term he adapted from the work of his close friend and professional confidant Henry Head.

Rather than supporting the warehouse metaphor of memory, where static traces or images are stored in the brain, Bartlett's studies pointed towards a more complex and nuanced picture. His participants didn't recall the stimulus material exactly or within its entirety, but reconstructed the material.

If the brain uses biological schema to constantly track and adjust physical posture based on past movements, thought Bartlett, it must use a cognitive schema to track, adjust, and interpret new information and experiences based on past knowledge.
Despite this choice, Bartlett writes: 'I strongly dislike the term "schema". It is at once too definite and too sketchy' (page 201-202).
By 1932, Bartlett's ideas were becoming eclipsed by behaviourism. Behaviourism discouraged all that could not be directly observed.

Researchers at Cambridge never stopped studying mental processes; their emphasis just shifted. So when Bartlett published Thinking in 1958, it wasn't part of a cognitive revolution, but rather a continuation of what Cambridge had been doing all along.

t: The Economics of Attention
q: Quite rightly, schools are meticulous about accounting for money, with every significant expenditure needing to be justified. Do time and attention deserve the same discipline?

According to William Ocasio, organisations become what their members collectively pay attention to. In schools, what leaders look for occupies teachers' minds, just as what teachers look for occupies students' minds.

Rubinstein, Meyer and Evans found that switching between tasks carries a reliable cognitive penalty. Each time we switch between tasks we not only lose time, we also increase the likelihood of mistakes.
Research has found that, after an interruption, knowledge workers took an average of 23 minutes and 15 seconds to return to their original task, often after completing several other tasks first.

This narrowing of attention results in an effect they call tunnelling: when a resource becomes scarce, immediate demands dominate our thinking, making it harder to focus on longer-term, more strategic concerns.
Creating more time certainly helps, but it won't result in more attentional capacity. Creating time is a scheduling challenge whereas as protecting attention is organisational design challenge.
If the answer's no, you may be accumulating attentional debt without generating attentional returns.

t: The Divide Was Already There
q: AI didn't fracture the campus. It found the fractures. Whether it widens them or heals them is the most consequential choice higher education will make this decade.

At the University of Maryland, AI-related misconduct cases jumped 59% in a single year. In an Inside Higher Ed survey, 85% of students said they'd used generative AI for coursework in the past year -- one in five to write entire essays.
A University of Chicago study found something devastating this year: about 60% of students admit to using AI, but they estimate 90% of their peers do.

This is the reframe I want to offer: AI doesn't divide campuses. It audits them. It finds every place where trust was already thin, where work was already performative, where governance was already theater.
As of April 2026, 0.7% of students had completed the voluntary AI training. A systemwide survey of 94,000 people found 52% of faculty saying AI had negatively affected their teaching.
At Harvard, a physics course's purpose-built AI tutor -- engineered to scaffold, not solve -- produced roughly double the learning gains of the same lesson delivered as in-class active learning.

AI will not strengthen your campus, any more than a bell strengthens a congregation. People strengthen campuses -- when a moment of shared disruption gives them a reason to renegotiate, out loud, what they owe each other.

t: Soma for the Classroom
q: In education, things are different. In that domain, the desire to remove friction is often counter-productive because it is in the discomfort that the learning happens.

A reward delivered on an unpredictable schedule, sometimes after one correct response, sometimes after several, produces behaviour far more persistent than a reward every time. This is the variable-ratio schedule.
Significantly, Skinner didn't use variable-ratio schedules in his own teaching machines, believing that classroom learning should be errorless and guided by continuous, immediate reinforcement.
The reason the gains are shallow and temporary is because gamification tends to weigh heavily on the absorption side of the balance and much less on the friction side.
Does it remove the productive struggle that creates the learning, or work that was never the point of it?
What it takes away from the learner is not fixed by what it is; it is decided, exchange by exchange, according to how it is used.
Like Soma, frictionless learning requires us to notice what is missing in the moment and then to insist on retaining the discomfort that keeps us learning because that is what keeps us human.

t: Retconning the Curriculum: Why the Science of Learning Has a Serious Design Problem
q: In the science of learning, the practice of retrieving previously learned material from memory is about the closest thing we have to penicillin in learning terms.

They have mutated from properties which exist to serve a curriculum into a range of techniques which give the impression of effective teaching but in reality, often grafted onto curricula never designed for them.

In 2020, Doug Rohrer and colleagues at the University of South Florida took several of the most used Maths textbooks in US schools and coded every problem (over 13,000 of them) against an ingenious question: does this practice problem require the student to retrieve anything from a previous chapter or does it just live inside the existing chapter?
For me, all this confirms the fact that the science of learning has far more to do with curriculum design than teaching activities.

A classroom full of kids raising mini-whiteboards like a Mexican wave might give the impression of learning but unless we examine closely what was being attended to then we risk the whole enterprise being pedagogical kayfabe.
To borrow again from Christine Counsell, retrieval practice without a destination or return path is an intransitive pedagogy, a pedagogy without an object.
The evidence never showed that quizzing strengthens memory per se; it showed that retrieval at a delay, timed against forgetting, strengthens memory.

Retconning the curriculum by bolting on the science of learning to materials that were never designed with them in mind might look evidence based but we will find out later if any learning actually took place, and probably too late.

t: Leadership Is Complex, Not Complicated
q: In a complicated system the total is the sum of the parts and knowing each part gives you a full understanding of the whole system, its behavior and output. Complicated problems have a "right" solution.
In a complex systems the total is more than the sum of its parts and knowing the single pieces is not enough to reliably predict how the system will behave.

Taylorism addressed the problem by removing its complex aspects: it transformed people into cogs of the factory process, forcing them to adhere to strict instructions, measuring their output with scientific precision and treating them as replaceable parts.
This approach failed miserably when applied to knowledge work, as removing judgment from a system that runs on judgment produced disengagement, output below expectations and a machine that grinds.

See the recent wave of mandated return to office (an attempt to summon collaboration by scheduling it, which will only obtain bodies at desks on Tuesdays) and the number of prescriptive dickheads still successfully climbing the corporate ladder.
People are complex. Embrace it. Own it. Treat them as such and you will be amazed at what they will achieve.

t: Know What You Carry: Principle 3 of The Way Through
q: A fresh start changes where you are or the company you keep, but it doesn't change what comes with you.

Growth and recovery are built on the understanding that unless we deliberately unpack and understand the beliefs, thoughts, and responses that we carry, they remain with us and will travel wherever we go.
Take someone who struggles with criticism at work. They feel singled out, believe feedback is unfair, and eventually leave because the workplace feels like the problem.
Then feedback arrives, and the same discomfort returns. Comments again feel personal, and the person again becomes defensive or starts questioning whether they are being treated fairly.
With awareness, you create a small gap between what happens and what you do next, and in that gap sits choice, the choice to grow.
Every construct we carry has history, but they don't all deserve a future. Several of mine felt like fixed parts of my personality for years.

Knowing what you carry doesn't mean living in the past. On the contrary, you only need to look back enough to understand what keeps turning up today, then turn your attention towards what you want to do next.

t: Introducing The Practice Project
q: I've argued for some time that if the initial impulse of the education reform movement was largely about changing systems, the next phase must focus on improving classroom practice.

Each paper in the series translates evidence from cognitive science, education research, and the accumulated wisdom of accomplished educators, thinkers, and writers into practical guidance for teachers, instructional coaches, and school leaders.

The inaugural essay, "Explicit Instruction Works. Education Schools Just Won't Admit It," by Zach Groshell, takes on one of the most persistent misconceptions in teacher education: that explicit instruction is somehow outdated or inferior to more "student-centered" approaches.
Daisy demonstrates why these abilities are far less transferable than we often imagine, arguing that critical thinking depends on knowledge rather than existing apart from it.

Notice that neither paper proposes a new law, a new accountability system, or a new governance structure. Instead, both ask a simpler--and ultimately more consequential--question: What should teachers know in order to help students learn?

I hope these papers become the education equivalent of those little manuals--not articles that are read once and forgotten, but resources teachers save, annotate, share with colleagues, and return to when they're wrestling with a familiar problem of practice.

t: How Emotion Changes What You See
q: You don't feel angry about what you saw. You see it through the anger. Most of us picture this the other way around.
Fear collapses your attention onto the threat, and whatever isn't the threat stops making it onto the map. You're not choosing this.
Anger doesn't only make it feel worse. It supplies a reason for it. Where fear left things off your map, this puts something on it that was never there.
That certainty is the giveaway, because you have no access to the inside of anyone's head. If your map has their reasoning on it, your map has fiction on it.
The experience of having a distorted map is not the experience of distortion. It's the experience of clarity. Sharper than usual, more certain than usual, everything suddenly fitting together.
The move is smaller. When you notice the state, go ahead and act. Send the reply, make the call, handle the thing. Just don't conclude yet.
Answer the email. Don't decide what kind of person they are.

t: Giving People the Reasons Behind Your Conclusions
q: When team members bring Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang a question, a stalled problem, or a possible opportunity, he doesn't just give them an answer or verdict. He also makes visible the steps that led him to his conclusion.
The leader who goes beyond "Let's do it" to explain how they decided is teaching people how to think.

Learning researchers call this reasoning-transferring process a "cognitive apprenticeship." By making hidden thinking processes explicit, leaders give people a window into how they use their experience to make better judgments.
Leaders not confident in their thinking can appear more subjective and uncertain in how they reach a decision, potentially undermining their credibility.
The reasoning behind a decision or conclusion is the only understanding that a team member can actually carry to the next question, the next problem, or the next opportunity.

t: Don't Talk At People
q: Communication is not the transfer of a thought from one head to another, because that is simply impossible. When you say something, you produce a set of words whose meaning is shaped by context, relationship, shared history and more.

The nod you get from your colleague doesn't mean that they have interpreted your words in the same way as you intended. More often than not, it just means they're tracking the conversation, which is quite a different thing.
Pre-loaded conclusions. You open a conversation by presenting the outcome you have already reached, inviting the other person into a conversation that is, functionally, already over.

Code-switching is the adjustment some people make to be taken seriously in that environment. They modify vocabulary, sentence structure, formality, accent and the degree of emotion they allow themselves to show.
Offer a candidate understanding. Paraphrase what you've heard as a test rather than a conclusion.
What we're after is a conversation that ends with both people holding a more reliable picture of reality than either had going in.

t: Comparing Fractions
q: Comparing fractions is a staple of most fraction stories. And the takeaway is usually a procedural understanding--whether the instruction is explicit or not: to compare fractions, ensure they are written with the same denominator; then compare the numerators.
In our story, 2 thirds compared with 4 thirds is like 2 meters compared with 4 meters. It is obvious, because the language we have built makes it so.

An 'inquiry routine' for review (that we expect students to be solid on) that functions to push critical thinking sounds to me like a great idea that should be repeated, evaluating mostly on a case-by-case basis.

Then we summarize, explain why, show some more examples, and move into practice--at least in this story, so far, before the minds of craft expert, research expert, design expert, have had a chance to tear it apart and put it back together.

What I continue to find interesting are all the ways that working on these stories reveal real conceptual tangles in instruction, and how thinking about how to get rid of those tangles actually decreases the need for handholding as the story progresses.

t: BMW Just Did Something Worth Reading Carefully
q: BMW agreed 8,000 job cuts this week, negotiated quietly with the works council, no rejected board vote, no public confrontation still to come. Where Volkswagen has been fighting the same scale of restructuring for months, BMW resolved it in weeks.
Look at where the cuts actually land. Not administration. Not back office. New model development. The engineering work that has always been BMW's real competitive edge over cheaper rivals.
What if a smaller number of highly capable people, working with significantly better tools, can now do what previously required a much larger specialist team around them?

This is the distinction between expertise at scale and Domain Mastery. Expertise at scale requires large teams because the knowledge is distributed across many people, each holding a piece of the picture.

If that second reading is right, it would not appear in a press release. It would look exactly like a routine cost-cutting story, right up until the moment the next generation of models arrived and the question answered itself.

t: 5 Theses Against AI Humanoid Teachers
q: If an impressionable young learner shares a classroom with a human looking, human sounding, and human feeling robot, we're giving them the poorest possible preparation for keeping the robot/human distinction clear in their minds.
Relating to students isn't something we outsource to make room for other things, it's the thing we make room for.

Theologian Andy Crouch argues we are "heart-soul-mind-strength complexes designed for love." You may or may not agree with his Christian perspective, but I hope it prompts you to see that treating learners as merely brains to be filled with facts is a mistake.
There is a clear and obvious line from AI teacher aides to AI teachers, and to encourage the former is to pave the way for the latter.

A seminal study by Cohen and Riel found that students writing for peers wrote better essays than when writing for teachers for a semester grade. It mattered to the students that someone would not just read, but desire to read their work.
Five theses, one big idea: humans should be educated by humans.

t: You Need to Work on Your Pace
q: I've heard this feedback given directly (to me, many years ago) and to others over the years. I've also heard it anecdotally from teachers recounting how their lesson observation went. And I think it represents a problem with lesson observations.
The observer assumes that their own processing speed (as an educated adult) is a reliable proxy for students' processing speed.
A pedagogical framework can be principle led, helping leaders to hold an evidence informed mental model of what makes great teaching to help make sense of what they are seeing in lesson observations.
A non specialist tasked with observing and feeding back can at best notice superficial features of practice or students' reactions to the flow of a lesson.

Going faster is unlikely to change the conditions required for learning to be more effective. Children need fluency practice, which could look like the lesson is going slower. They need opportunities to recall prior knowledge and make connections; going faster only benefits the students who do this quickest.

A teacher trying to act on the feedback of increasing pace without considering task design, modelling, scaffolding etc will likely experience frustration. Better designed examples for modelling might enable quicker grasping of content. Better faded scaffolding might enable students to more quickly internalise processes.

I think that what looks like a pace problem is almost certainly something else upstream. Furthermore and more importantly, if pace is the feedback of lesson observations, I'd argue more work needs to be done on the concept of lesson observations and their developmental and evaluative use among the leadership team.

t: Learning Hard Skills Takes Years
q: For most of my career, I was trained as a delivery expert. Scope, schedule, budget. Build the thing on time, on specifications, and on budget. That's what the project managers' guide teaches you. But the highest-stakes work require something else on top of that. A set of skills nobody handed me a credential for.

Most PM education stops at strategy. Align the portfolio. Check the box. Done. Elite level is different. The environment keeps shifting under you. The people you need aren't your reports, they don't answer to you at all.

Complex adaptive systems are different. It requires navigating emergence, human behavior, politics, diplomacy, and high ambiguity, how to survive and steer when the environment itself is fluid and unpredictable, and the ground keeps shifting under the plan.
This is the cluster that convinced me this is a different job, not a harder version of the same one. At this level, nobody hands you a governance structure. You have to build it.
Traditional program management assumes a monocentric hierarchy, one sponsor, one chain of command. Large joint ventures and public-private partnerships don't work that way.

None of these are PM-specific once you look closely and mostly used in other professional domains. Cynefin, Wardley mapping, polycentric governance, the OODA loop: none of it was built for project managers. It was built for people who need to see structure, power, layers, environments, and change clearly, whatever field they're in.
I've spent 15-plus years managing federal programs. Polycentric governance and metagovernance aren't theory to me. They're what cross-agency IT modernization work forces you to learn, or fail at.

t: 4 Quality Assurance Traps to Avoid
q: We can only gain an insight through proxies because learning is largely invisible and happens over time. The problem is that what we might commonly look for and notice when we're doing quality assurance work are poor proxies:

Leaders can have a pretty skewed view of school life because we change others' behaviours simply by being there. It is far more useful to try and understand the underlying beliefs, assumptions and values of colleagues because they sustain actions.

While the rubric may have been helpful to draw attention to specific practices that we want teachers to work on, they can ultimately limit practice and provide us with a skewed view on the reality of school life because they could oversimplify the complex to the extent that practices lacks nuance and responsiveness.
Catching misconceptions early through checking for understanding here can help leaders to intervene before habits become embedded and time is lost.
We can only learn what we think about and we can only think about what we are paying attention to, so as early warning systems go, attention is first pick.

Not only are measurements of learning likely to be unreliable, but, as Muller argues, the practice of measuring itself can have negative effects on climate. Muller talks of a toxic cycle measuring leading to mistrust and mistrust leading to more measurement. All the more reason to focus more on mapping, rather than weighing.

It is often the person closes to the problem that has the most useful insights - leaders are often removed from the reality of problems because they influence others with their very presences and truth does not often rise to the top.
We must treat our assumptions as hypotheses to be tested rather than truths to be confirmed.

t: The Qualities of a Great Teammate
q: Being the teammate everyone wants to work with is a career asset that appreciates over time.
Because the best learning in organizations comes from peers, not training programs, great teammates receive more insights, best practices, and candid feedback.
They understand the difference between voicing dissent before a decision is made and undermining it afterward.
Every quality described here, from dependability to full commitment, is really a form of leadership practiced without permission or authority.
Great teammates are those leaders. The title eventually catches up to them.

t: Standards Are Not It
q: A content analysis is the search for generative relations inside a content domain, and the arrangement of the content so those relations become the organizing structure of the course.
A relation is generative to the degree that learning it lets a student respond correctly to items nobody taught them.
Spelling Through Morphographs teaches 750 morphographs and 14 rules, and students can derive the spelling of over 12,000 words.

Four rules and 36 families instead of 200 items. And the families keep paying out well past the fact table, because another invisible sameness in the content is that a word problem in the primary grades is just a family with one member missing.
Convection is the big idea, and all these topics are its instances.

Slocum and Rolf (2021) name the problem directly: instructional designs derived from skill assessments tend to omit the step of identifying the generative relations that would produce the repertoire the assessments sample.
An assessment tells you which behaviors a student can perform. It does not tell you how to organize a course that is economical and intellectually rigorous.

We cannot keep setting the bar this low, where a course counts as good if someone fed a standards document to a large language model, churned out a lesson for every entry, and called the result a curriculum.
Standards are the right tool for checking coverage once a course is built. They are the wrong tool for deciding what the lessons are.

t: Returning to Key Stage 3: A Curriculum Begins With an Entitlement
q: I began this work by refining our approach to assessment, but it took me further back: to what every student should gain from studying the subject in the first place.
By entitlement, I mean the knowledge, disciplinary thinking and growing independence that every student should have the opportunity to develop.
Until teachers can answer that, ‘Secure’ risks becoming a polished reporting label rather than a meaningful judgement.
Entitlement provides the reference point. It connects assessment to the curriculum, rather than leaving it as a separate exercise in reporting.

A curriculum can appear organised because all the required documents exist. Coherence becomes visible when one part of the learning prepares students for what follows and when teachers understand why a text, concept or task belongs where it does.

Students in one may build knowledge they can draw on when they meet a new text, recognise connections and make more of the decisions for themselves. In other settings, the taught units may be worthwhile but remain separate in students’ minds, recalled for the assessment and then quietly left behind.
Education should enlarge the world available to students. Familiarity has a place, but it cannot set the boundary of what students encounter at school.
Schools should return to the model each year. Continual review does not mean replacing everything whenever an imperfection appears.
These questions will not make the curriculum decisions for a department. They do, however, establish what must come before a meaningful account of progression.

t: How to Design Around Cognitive Offloading
q: When students used AI as a replacement for their own thinking — paste the assignment in, take what comes out — the two highest forms of thinking (judging the quality of ideas, and building on them) appeared exactly zero times.
The reason: when the AI judges first, learners stop judging their own work and simply edit the AI’s opinion. The evaluating — the part that builds the skill — had been handed over (Ates, 2026).

Students who dabbled with AI — fix a sentence here, check a fact there — learned less than students who used no AI at all. Dabblers carried all of the mental workload themselves, plus the extra effort of managing the tool, and freed up no capacity for deeper thinking.

The winning design added one small step: before the AI’s feedback opened, students spent two minutes judging their own draft — strongest point, weakest point, one thing they were unsure about, top revision priority.

On that delayed test, the AI-based designs finished both last and first, with human-only feedback in the middle. Same tool, same model, same prompts. So is AI feedback better than human feedback turns out to be the wrong question.

Students who handed entire categories of supporting work to AI — summarising sources, first-pass literature reviews, organising data — and then spent the freed time on what AI can't do for them showed the deepest learning in the study.
AI can support and enhance human cognition when — and only when — the human retains cognitive ownership. Each study conducted so far has located that ownership at three different levels of design.
Ownership has to be designed into the task and reinforced through practice — made the path of least resistance, not an act of learner virtue.

t: Shakespeare and the Classics

t: How to Read Different Kinds of Books
